lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Crop science aspects: agronomy, crop pathology and entomology (Week 1 supplement)
objectives: Define agronomy as the science of crop production and soil management.
Define crop pathology and explain that it studies diseases affecting crops and other plants.
Define entomology and describe its relevance to harmful and beneficial insects in agriculture.
Distinguish crop pathology from veterinary pathology.
lessons.body:
Week 1 Supplement: Three Crop-Science Disciplines

The Week 1 source lists agronomy, crop pathology and entomology as aspects of crop production but does not define them. This supplement explains what each discipline studies and how each helps farming.

## 1. Agronomy

Agronomy is the science of crop production and soil management. It studies how crops grow and how soil and field conditions affect them. Agronomists consider matters such as crop choice, soil properties, planting practices, crop rotation, weed management and ways to maintain productive soil. Their work helps farmers make informed decisions about growing crops and caring for the land.

## 2. Crop Pathology

Crop pathology, also called plant pathology when the subject is plants generally, is the study of diseases that affect crops. It investigates what causes plant diseases, how they develop and spread, the damage they cause, and how they can be prevented or managed. Causes may include fungi, bacteria, viruses, plant-parasitic nematodes and harmful non-living conditions such as nutrient imbalance or air pollutants.

For example, when maize or cassava plants show signs of disease, crop pathology helps identify the cause and understand how the disease affects the crop.

**Important distinction:** Crop pathology deals with diseases of plants and crops. Diseases of farm animals belong to veterinary pathology. The source's broader description of pathology as covering both crops and animals should not be used as the definition of crop pathology.

## 3. Entomology

Entomology is the scientific study of insects. Agricultural entomology applies this knowledge to farming. Some insects damage crops by feeding on leaves, stems, roots, flowers or stored produce. Other insects are useful: bees and other pollinators help some crops produce fruits and seeds, while predatory insects feed on crop pests.

An entomologist studies insects, their identification, life cycles, behaviour and effects on crops. This knowledge helps farmers recognise harmful insects and protect beneficial ones.

## How the Three Disciplines Work Together

Consider a maize field:
- An agronomist considers the crop, soil and field practices needed for good growth.
- A crop pathologist investigates a disease affecting the maize plants.
- An entomologist identifies insects feeding on the crop or insects that help control those pests.

The disciplines are related, but they ask different questions: agronomy focuses on crop production and soil management; crop pathology focuses on crop diseases; entomology focuses on insects.

## Key Points to Remember

- Agronomy: science of crop production and soil management.
- Crop pathology: study of diseases affecting crops and other plants.
- Entomology: scientific study of insects, including harmful and beneficial insects.
- Veterinary pathology, not crop pathology, is the specialist field concerned with animal diseases.

practice.question: Define each of the following: (a) agronomy; (b) crop pathology; (c) entomology.
practice.answer: (a) Agronomy is the science of crop production and soil management. (b) Crop pathology is the study of diseases affecting crops and other plants, including their causes, development and management. (c) Entomology is the scientific study of insects.

marking.criterion: Defines agronomy as the science of crop production and soil management.
Defines crop pathology as the study of diseases affecting crops/plants.
Defines entomology as the scientific study of insects.

practice.question: A farmer notices a disease affecting cassava leaves and caterpillars feeding on maize leaves. Name the discipline that investigates each problem and give a reason for each choice.
practice.answer: Crop pathology investigates the disease affecting cassava because it studies diseases of crops. Agricultural entomology investigates the caterpillars because they are insects and entomology studies insects that affect crops.

marking.criterion: Identifies crop pathology for the cassava disease and explains that it studies crop diseases.
Identifies agricultural entomology for the caterpillars and explains that they are insects.

practice.question: A learner says that crop pathology is the study of diseases of crops and farm animals. Correct the statement and name the specialist field concerned with animal diseases.
practice.answer: Crop pathology studies diseases of crops and other plants. Diseases of farm animals are studied in veterinary pathology.

marking.criterion: States that crop pathology concerns diseases of crops/plants.
Names veterinary pathology as the specialist field concerned with animal diseases.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 1 keyed practice: answers and marking guide (supplement)
objectives: Provide complete answers to the Week 1 evaluation, general evaluation, weekend assignment and theory questions using taught source content.
Apply the source's definitions of agriculture, branches, importance and agro-based industries, including the Week 6 cross-week material where required.
Explain where the source gives no ranking and where its use of agro-allied/agro-based terminology is inconsistent.
lessons.body:
Week 1 Supplement: Keyed Practice and Marking Guide

This guide provides suggested answers and criterion-level marking for the Week 1 evaluation, general evaluation, weekend assignment and theory questions. Answers are based on the First Term teaching blocks and the Week 1 crop-science supplement. The Week 6 teaching blocks are used where the Week 1 questions depend on agro-based or agro-allied industries.

The source does not state a ranking for the most important reason for practising agriculture. For the weekend multiple-choice question, food is the reasoned sample choice because food is essential for human and animal life; this is a justified answer, not a ranking quoted from the source.

The Week 6 text at block 482 uses “agro-allied industries” and “agro-based industries” for industries that depend on agriculture for raw materials, and block 486 gives examples. Week 1 block 105 also uses “agro-allied” for suppliers of farm inputs. These uses are inconsistent in the source. For questions that depend on the Week 6 definition and table, this answer key follows the explicit Week 6 definition and records the inconsistency rather than silently treating the terms as universally interchangeable.

For the weekend multiple-choice item about diseases of crops and animals, the option “Pathology” is answered as written. This general term is distinct from “crop pathology,” which the Week 1 crop-science supplement defines as the study of diseases affecting crops and other plants; animal diseases belong to veterinary pathology.

practice.question: Answer the Week 1 evaluation questions: (a) define agriculture; (b) name the two Latin words from which the term is derived and give their meanings; (c) define agronomy, crop pathology and entomology; (d) state three functions each of veterinary medicine and agricultural extension; (e) define agro-based industries.
practice.answer: (a) Agriculture is the art and science or management of cultivating crops and rearing animals for human use, including the production and handling of plant and animal products. (b) Ager means field, farm or land; the source writes Culture in block 58 and Cultura in the weekend MCQ, both meaning cultivation. (c) Agronomy: the science of crop production and soil management. Crop pathology: the study of diseases affecting crops and other plants. Entomology: the scientific study of insects. (d) Veterinary medicine: improves the health management of farm animals; helps control pests; helps control parasites and animal diseases. Agricultural extension: trains farmers; disseminates agricultural information; links farmers with researchers. (e) Using the Week 6 definition, agro-based industries are industries that depend on agricultural raw materials to operate and produce goods.

marking.criterion: Defines agriculture and includes crop cultivation.
Includes rearing of animals and the production/handling of plant and animal products.
States Ager means field, farm or land.
States Culture/Cultura means cultivation and notes the source's spelling variation.
Defines agronomy as crop production and soil management.
Defines crop pathology as study of diseases affecting crops/plants.
Defines entomology as the scientific study of insects.
Gives veterinary health management as one function.
Gives pest control as a veterinary function.
Gives parasite and/or disease control as a veterinary function.
Gives farmer training as an extension function.
Gives dissemination of agricultural information as an extension function.
Gives linking farmers with researchers as an extension function.
Defines agro-based industries as depending on agricultural raw materials.

practice.question: Answer the Week 1 importance evaluation: (a) outline five importance of agriculture; (b) give five examples of agro-based industries; (c) state five agricultural raw materials and the industries that use them.
practice.answer: (a) Any five: food; materials for clothing; materials for shelter and furniture; income; employment; raw materials for industries; foreign exchange; market for industrial goods; rural development; recreation and tourism. (b) Any five from the Week 6 table: Oil mill; Soap industry; Textile/ginnery; Brewery; Paper industry. (c) Cotton — textile industry. Wool — textile industry. Cocoa — beverage industry. Coffee — beverage industry. Rubber latex — tyre and foam industries. These examples are taken from Week 1 block 103 and Week 6 table block 486.

marking.criterion: Gives five distinct importance of agriculture from blocks 98-107 (one mark each).
Gives five valid agro-based industry examples from Week 6 block 486 (one mark each).
Gives five correct agricultural raw materials (one mark each).
Matches each raw material with its correct industry (one mark each).

practice.question: Answer the Week 1 general evaluation: (a) define agriculture; (b) list and define any eight branches of agriculture; (c) define agro-allied industries as used in Week 6 and give five examples; (d) state five agricultural raw materials and their industries; (e) state ten relevance of agriculture; (f) define agronomy, crop pathology and entomology.
practice.answer: (a) Agriculture is the art and science or management of cultivating crops and rearing animals for human use, including production and handling of plant and animal products. (b) Any eight of the following: 1. Animal Science/Animal Husbandry/Animal Production: Ensures effective management of farm animals and better animal productivity. 2. Veterinary Medicine/Animal Health: Provides better health management for farm animals and controls pests, parasites and animal diseases. 3. Soil Science: Maintains soil fertility, supports soil classification and mapping, and helps control erosion and conserve soil moisture. 4. Crop Production/Crop Science: Supports effective crop management and the development/use of better planting materials and correct crop spacing. 5. Agricultural Economics and Farm Management: Supports effective management of agricultural resources, agricultural marketing and farm accounting. 6. Agricultural Engineering: Promotes mechanisation, develops processing and storage equipment, and maintains farm tools and equipment. 7. Agricultural Extension and Education: Trains farmers, disseminates agricultural information and links farmers with researchers. 8. Forestry and Wildlife Conservation: Promotes conservation of forest products and wildlife and helps create a suitable microclimate. (c) In Week 6 block 482, agro-allied/agro-based industries are industries that depend on agriculture for raw materials. Five examples: Oil mill, Soap industry, Textile/ginnery, Brewery, Paper industry. (d) Cotton — textile industry. Wool — textile industry. Cocoa — beverage industry. Coffee — beverage industry. Rubber latex — tyre and foam industries. (e) Provision of food for people and farm animals. Supply of materials for clothing, such as cotton, fibre, hides and skins. Supply of materials for shelter and furniture, such as timber. Generation of income from the sale of crops and animal products and from agricultural wages. Employment for farmers, farm workers and people in agricultural finance and marketing. Supply of raw materials for industries, such as cotton, cocoa and rubber latex. Generation of foreign exchange through exports of agricultural products. Provision of a market for industrial goods used in agriculture. Development of rural areas through roads, electricity, water, schools and hospitals. Provision of facilities for recreation and tourism, including game reserves and horse-related activities. (f) Agronomy: the science of crop production and soil management. Crop pathology: the study of diseases affecting crops and other plants. Entomology: the scientific study of insects.

marking.criterion: Defines agriculture as crop cultivation and animal rearing for human use.
Lists and defines eight correct branches: one mark for each branch name and one for its function.
Defines agro-allied industries according to Week 6 block 482 as industries dependent on agricultural raw materials.
Gives five valid examples from Week 6 block 486.
Gives five correct agricultural raw materials.
Matches each raw material to its correct industry.
States ten distinct importance/relevance points from blocks 98-107.
Defines agronomy, crop pathology and entomology (two marks each).

practice.question: Answer the five Week 1 weekend multiple-choice questions (blocks 127-136). Give the correct option for each.
practice.answer: 1. C — Ager means field/farm/land and Cultura means cultivation. The source spells the second word “Culture” in block 58 and “Cultura” in block 127; the meanings point to option C. 2. B — Entomology is the study of insects. 3. C — Pathology is the broad term used in the question for the study of diseases of crops and animals; crop pathology specifically concerns plants, while animal diseases belong to veterinary pathology. 4. B — Food. This is a reasoned choice because food is essential for human and animal life; the source lists food as an importance but does not explicitly rank it above the others. 5. C — Electronics. The Week 6 table lists soap, textile and paper industries among agro-based examples, but not electronics.

marking.criterion: Selects C for Q1 (field/cultivation).
Selects B for Q2 (Entomology).
Selects C for Q3 (Pathology).
Selects B for Q4 (Food); accept the sample reason if an explanation is requested, without claiming the source ranks it.
Selects C for Q5 (Electronics).

practice.question: Answer Theory Question 1: (a) define agriculture; (b) state ten importance of agriculture.
practice.answer: (a) Agriculture is the art and science or management of cultivating crops and rearing animals for human use, including the production and handling of plant and animal products. (b) The ten importance are: Provision of food for people and farm animals. Supply of materials for clothing, such as cotton, fibre, hides and skins. Supply of materials for shelter and furniture, such as timber. Generation of income from the sale of crops and animal products and from agricultural wages. Generation of foreign exchange through exports of agricultural products. Provision of a market for industrial goods used in agriculture. Development of rural areas through roads, electricity, water, schools and hospitals. Provision of facilities for recreation and tourism, including game reserves and horse-related activities.

marking.criterion: Defines agriculture by including crop cultivation and animal rearing for human use.
States ten distinct importance from blocks 98-107, one mark each.

practice.question: Answer Theory Question 2: list and define any ten branches of agriculture.
practice.answer: Any ten of the eleven branches taught in blocks 67-90 are acceptable. Sample answer: 1. Animal Science/Animal Husbandry/Animal Production: Ensures effective management of farm animals and better animal productivity. 2. Veterinary Medicine/Animal Health: Provides better health management for farm animals and controls pests, parasites and animal diseases. 3. Soil Science: Maintains soil fertility, supports soil classification and mapping, and helps control erosion and conserve soil moisture. 4. Crop Production/Crop Science: Supports effective crop management and the development/use of better planting materials and correct crop spacing. 5. Agricultural Economics and Farm Management: Supports effective management of agricultural resources, agricultural marketing and farm accounting. 6. Agricultural Engineering: Promotes mechanisation, develops processing and storage equipment, and maintains farm tools and equipment. 7. Agricultural Extension and Education: Trains farmers, disseminates agricultural information and links farmers with researchers. 8. Forestry and Wildlife Conservation: Promotes conservation of forest products and wildlife and helps create a suitable microclimate. 9. Fishery: Covers fish production, management, processing and fishing practices. 10. Apiculture/Bee Farming: Involves the production of honey.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 2 assessment supplement: simple farm tools and complex farm machines
objectives: Identify at least ten simple farm tools and state their uses.
Identify at least ten complex farm machines and state their uses.
Distinguish hand-operated tools from powered machines and tractor-operated implements.
lessons.body:
Week 2 Assessment Supplement: Simple Farm Tools and Complex Farm Machines

This is an assessment supplement for the Week 2 questions asking for ten simple farm tools and ten complex farm machines. It expands the examples in the source; it is not new scheme text or a replacement for the original lesson.

## 1. Simple Farm Tools

A simple farm tool is a hand-operated implement. The farmer supplies the effort directly, without an engine. Such tools are commonly used on small farms and in subsistence farming because they are relatively simple and can be used for small jobs. They are not limited to subsistence farms: commercial farms also use hand tools for particular tasks.

Examples and uses:
1. Cutlass or machete: clears weeds and light vegetation and cuts small stems or branches.
2. Hoe: loosens soil, removes weeds, makes furrows and forms small mounds.
3. Axe: cuts or splits wood and removes larger branches.
4. Spade: cuts into soil and digs planting holes or beds.
5. Shovel: scoops and moves soil, compost, manure or other loose materials.
6. Rake: gathers plant residues and weeds and helps level a seedbed.
7. Sickle: cuts grasses and weeds and can harvest small cereal crops.
8. Hand fork: loosens soil, removes weeds and turns compost around plants.
9. Hand trowel: loosens soil around plants and makes small holes for transplanting seedlings.
10. Watering can or manual sprinkler: applies water to nursery plants and young crops.
11. Wheelbarrow: carries soil, manure, seedlings, harvested produce and tools.
12. Mattock or pick-mattock: breaks hard ground and helps remove roots or stumps.
13. Secateurs or pruning shears: cut small stems and branches when pruning.
14. Hand cultivator: loosens the surface soil and removes weeds in garden plots.

## 2. Complex Farm Machines

A complex farm machine is mechanised equipment powered by an engine, electricity or hydraulic power. It can perform larger or heavier jobs more quickly than a hand tool and is commonly used in commercial farming. Some machines move under their own power; others are powered by a tractor or another machine.

Ten examples and uses:
1. Tractor: supplies power for pulling or pushing farm implements and for hauling trailers or materials.
2. Bulldozer: clears land, pushes vegetation and helps level ground.
3. Mechanical planter: places seeds in prepared soil at suitable depth and spacing.
4. Harvester: gathers mature crops over large areas more quickly than manual harvesting.
5. Power tiller: an engine-powered machine used for soil cultivation and other field operations on farms.
6. Self-propelled power weeder: removes weeds and performs inter-row cultivation in row crops.
7. Power-operated knapsack sprayer: applies liquid sprays to crops; powered versions use an engine or electric motor.
8. High-capacity multicrop thresher: separates grain from harvested crop heads or stalks and helps clean the grain.
9. Power-operated coconut dehusker: removes the outer husk from coconuts.
10. Irrigation pump unit: pumps water from a source to fields or an irrigation system.

## 3. Tractor-Operated Implements

Some mechanised farm equipment is an implement rather than a self-propelled machine. It is attached to or drawn by a tractor or power tiller, which supplies the power. Examples include:
- Tractor-drawn disc plough: cuts and turns soil during primary tillage.
- Tractor-mounted disc harrow: breaks soil clods and prepares a seedbed.
- Seed-cum-fertilizer drill: places seed and fertilizer in prepared rows.
- Tractor-drawn ridger: forms furrows and ridges for row crops.
- Tractor-operated post-hole digger: digs holes for planting tree seedlings.
- Power-tiller-mounted orchard sprayer: applies spray to foliage in orchard crops.

A tractor is a self-propelled machine; a disc plough or seed drill is an implement powered or drawn by the tractor. Farm-mechanisation lessons often teach them together because they form part of the machinery system.

## 4. Main Differences

- Power: a simple tool is operated mainly by human effort; a complex machine uses an engine, electricity, hydraulic power or a tractor.
- Scale: simple tools are suited to small jobs and plots; machines can handle larger areas, heavier loads or repeated operations.
- Speed and labour: hand tools usually require more physical effort and take longer; machines can complete many operations faster and reduce manual labour.
- Cost and upkeep: simple tools generally cost less and need simpler maintenance; machines usually require more capital, fuel or electricity, skilled operation and servicing.

These are common patterns, not absolute rules. A smallholder may hire a tractor, and a commercial farmer may still use a cutlass or hand trowel for a particular job.

lessons.title: Week 2 cross-week revision supplement: agro-based industries and raw materials
objectives: Explain agro-based industries and identify the agricultural raw materials they process.
Give at least five distinct agro-based industries and match each to its raw material.
Distinguish agro-based processing industries from agro-allied input-supply and support industries, noting the source's inconsistent terminology.
lessons.body:
Week 2 Cross-Week Revision Supplement: Agro-Based Industries, Agro-Allied Industries and Raw Materials

This is a cross-week revision supplement for the Week 2 questions about agro-based industries and the raw materials they use. It draws on the Week 1 teaching about agro-allied industries and the Week 6 examples of industries and raw materials. It is not a new Week 2 scheme objective or a replacement for the original source.

## 1. Agro-Based Industries

An agro-based industry processes raw materials obtained from agriculture, forestry or fisheries into finished or partly finished products. The raw material may come from crops, animals, trees or fish.

Examples and raw materials:
1. Textile or cotton-ginnery industry: cotton.
2. Beverage industry: cocoa, tea, coffee or kola nuts.
3. Soap industry: oil seeds and vegetable oils.
4. Paper industry: pulpwood or other suitable wood.
5. Sugar industry: sugarcane.
6. Flour mill: cereal grains such as wheat, maize, millet or sorghum.
7. Brewery: cereal grains such as barley, maize or sorghum.
8. Fruit-canning or juice industry: fruits such as mango, orange or pineapple.
9. Tyre and rubber-products industry: natural rubber latex.
10. Oil mill: oil seeds such as groundnut, soybean or palm kernels.

## 2. Agro-Allied Industries

In the Week 1 source, agro-allied industries are described as industries that supply goods or services needed for farming. They support agricultural production rather than processing harvested farm produce as their main activity.

Examples include:
- Fertilizer manufacturers and blenders, which supply plant nutrients.
- Pesticide and herbicide manufacturers, which supply crop-protection products.
- Agricultural machinery and equipment manufacturers or suppliers, which provide tractors, planters, pumps and other equipment.
- Animal-feed manufacturers, which supply feed for livestock and poultry.
- Seed companies, which supply planting materials.
- Irrigation-equipment and pump suppliers, which provide equipment for moving water to farms.
- Veterinary-drug and animal-health service providers, which support livestock health.

## 3. The Difference

- Agro-based industries process agricultural raw materials into products. Examples are a cotton textile mill, a paper mill or a sugar factory.
- Agro-allied industries supply inputs, equipment or services that help farmers produce crops and livestock. Examples are a fertilizer factory, a farm-machinery manufacturer or an animal-feed factory.

The terms are not used consistently in every source. Week 1 block 105 uses agro-allied for farm-input suppliers, while Week 6 block 482 writes “agro-allied/agro-based” together for industries using agricultural raw materials. FAO describes agro-industries broadly as including both upstream input/equipment supply and downstream processing. For clarity in this supplement, “agro-based” means the processing industries, while “agro-allied” means the input-supply/support industries, following the Week 1 distinction. The Week 6 wording is recorded as a source inconsistency rather than repeated as if the terms were identical.

## 4. How Agriculture and Industry Support Each Other

Agriculture supplies raw materials to agro-based processors. Agro-allied suppliers provide farmers with inputs and equipment. Industries also provide a market for farm produce, while farms provide food and raw materials for industrial workers and factories.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 3 supplement: roles of agricultural extension in agricultural development
objectives: Define agricultural extension as a service linking farmers with knowledge, skills, advice, research and support services.
Describe at least six roles of agricultural extension in agricultural development.
Explain how extension connects research institutions and farmers in both directions.
lessons.body:
Week 3 Supplement: Roles of Agricultural Extension in Agricultural Development

Agricultural extension is a service that connects farmers and rural communities with useful agricultural knowledge, skills, advice, research and support services. Extension agents work with farmers: they listen to farmers' needs, share information and help farmers make informed decisions.

The Week 3 source states that extension agents teach farmers improved methods of farming (block 273). This supplement explains additional roles supported by Nigerian agricultural research and extension institutions and international agricultural-development organisations.

## Main Roles of Agricultural Extension

1. **Teaching and training farmers:** Extension agents explain improved crop and livestock practices and help farmers build practical skills.
2. **Demonstrating improved methods:** They organise or support demonstration plots and practical sessions so farmers can see how a method or technology works.
3. **Sharing research and innovations:** They communicate research findings, improved varieties, new technologies and useful information in language farmers can understand.
4. **Providing advice and helping solve problems:** They help farmers identify production challenges and seek suitable advice from specialists, research institutes or relevant services.
5. **Connecting farmers and researchers:** They carry useful research information to farmers and communicate farmers' questions, experiences and problems back to researchers. This makes extension a two-way link.
6. **Linking farmers to markets and services:** They help farmers find information and connections relating to markets, farm inputs, credit, veterinary services and other support.
7. **Encouraging sustainable and climate-resilient farming:** They share information about soil and water conservation, biodiversity, climate adaptation and responsible production.
8. **Providing timely information through communication channels:** They use meetings, radio, mobile phones, helplines and digital platforms to make useful agricultural information easier to obtain.

## Example

A maize farmer notices an unfamiliar problem in the field and is unsure how to reach buyers. An extension agent can listen to the farmer, help record and describe the problem, seek advice from a research or specialist service, explain reliable information to the farmer, and help connect the farmer with relevant input or market services. The agent can also report the farmer's experience to the research system. The extension agent does not replace a researcher, veterinarian or buyer; the agent helps farmers reach the right knowledge and services.

## Key Point

Agricultural extension is more than giving instructions. It involves teaching, demonstration, advice, information-sharing and links among farmers, researchers, markets and support services. Information also flows back from farmers so that research and services can respond to real farming needs.

objectives: Define pesticide, herbicide, weedicide and insecticide.
Distinguish herbicides from the broader pesticide category and from insecticides, fungicides and rodenticides.

lessons.body:
Week 3 Terminology Supplement: Herbicide and Related Pesticide Terms

This supplement explains the terms needed for the Week 3 weekend question about the substance used to control weeds. It provides definitions only. It does not give product recommendations, application instructions, rates, doses, mixing directions or handling advice.

## 1. Pesticide

A pesticide is a broad term for a substance or mixture intended to prevent, destroy, repel or control a pest. Pesticides include several groups, such as herbicides, insecticides, fungicides and rodenticides. Some pesticide products may be chemical or biological.

## 2. Herbicide

A herbicide is a type of pesticide used to destroy or control unwanted plants, especially weeds. It is the specific term for a weed-control product.

## 3. Weedicide

Weedicide is another name for a herbicide. Both terms refer to an agent used to control weeds. It is not a different target group from herbicide.

## 4. Insecticide

An insecticide is a type of pesticide used to kill or control insects. It targets insects, not weeds.

## 5. Other Related Terms

- Fungicide: a pesticide used to control fungi.
- Rodenticide: a pesticide used to control rodents such as rats and mice.

## 6. Answering the Week 3 Multiple-Choice Question

The source asks which chemical is used to destroy weeds and offers both **herbicide** (option A) and **weedicide** (option C). These are synonyms. Therefore, both A and C are correct in meaning. “Herbicide” is the standard technical term, but “weedicide” is also a recognised name for a weed-control agent. The question does not have one unique correct option as printed. A fair answer key should accept A or C; if only one option is to be correct in a future version, the assessment writer should replace one of the duplicate choices.

Remember: pesticide is the broad group; herbicide/weedicide controls weeds; insecticide controls insects. This supplement is terminology teaching only and gives no instructions for selecting, buying, mixing, applying, storing or handling pesticide products.

lessons.title: Week 4 assessment supplement: NGOs contributing to agricultural development in Nigeria
objectives: Name five non-governmental or non-profit development organisations with verified agricultural work in Nigeria.
Describe one agricultural contribution of each organisation.
State roles NGOs can play in agricultural development and distinguish this Nigeria-focused supplement from the original source list.
lessons.body:
Week 4 Assessment Supplement: NGOs Contributing to Agricultural Development in Nigeria

This supplement adds five organisations with verified agricultural work in Nigeria. It is separate from, and does not replace, the original source list at blocks 387-392. That list is preserved as printed: it names the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture, West African Rice Development Agency, Food and Agriculture Organization, The Hunger Project (Ghana) and Catholic Relief Service (Gambia). The supplement does not silently change the countries or status stated in the source.

## Five Nigeria-Relevant Organisations

1. **Sasakawa Africa Association (SAA-Nigeria):** Works with Nigerian agricultural extension services, extension workers and smallholder farmers. Its activities include training, improved crop practices, demonstration plots, climate-resilient farming, post-harvest support and stronger links to markets.
2. **Heifer International Nigeria:** Supports smallholder farmers, women and young people with skills, technical guidance, access to resources, finance, insurance and market connections. Its Nigerian work includes dairy, fruits and vegetables, poultry, rice and small-ruminant value chains.
3. **TechnoServe Nigeria:** Supports agricultural value chains including maize, rice, cashew, tomato, cassava, soy and poultry. Its work aims to improve smallholder productivity and income, access to farm inputs and finance, and connections to markets.
4. **Catholic Relief Services (CRS) Nigeria:** Works in agriculture, livelihoods and resilience. It supports households, communities and farmer groups to increase agricultural production and diversify incomes; its Nigeria work has also supported cassava seed entrepreneurs and planting-material markets.
5. **Women Farmers Advancement Network (WOFAN):** A Nigerian non-profit organisation that supports smallholder farmers, particularly women and young people. Its work includes agricultural community projects, training of extension workers, farmer empowerment and climate-related information and resilience.

## How NGOs Contribute to Agriculture

The Week 4 source identifies six contribution areas:
- Research: finding solutions to agricultural problems and supporting improved crops or livestock.
- Finance: supporting agricultural projects.
- Inputs: helping farmers obtain items such as fertilizers, pesticides and other farm inputs.
- Extension services: improving farmers' knowledge through information, training and advice.
- Rural development: supporting basic facilities and services in rural communities.
- Irrigation and drainage: helping make water available or manage excess water for agricultural production.

Different organisations specialise in different areas. The five examples above are included because their own records show agricultural work in Nigeria; they should not be treated as having identical programmes.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 4 supplement: Nigerian agricultural programmes and their objectives
objectives: Name at least five Nigerian agricultural programmes or schemes and state two programme-specific objectives for each.
Identify the Farm Settlement Scheme as the programme designed to attract educated young people into farming and explain the historical evidence.
Distinguish broad national agricultural policy goals from the specific objectives of named programmes.
lessons.body:
Week 4 Supplement: Nigerian Agricultural Programmes and Their Objectives

A government agricultural policy states broad goals for the country. An agricultural programme is a planned way of working towards one or more of those goals. A programme has its own specific objectives; the broad goals of agricultural policy should not be copied as if they were the objectives of every programme.

## Five Nigerian Agricultural Programmes

1. **Farm Settlement Scheme (historical):**
   - Encourage educated young people and school leavers to choose modern farming as a career.
   - Establish planned farm settlements that demonstrate viable farming and support rural progress. The historical Western Region scheme included farm-institute training, allocation of farm holdings and supervised financial assistance.

2. **Agricultural Development Projects (ADPs):**
   - Increase agricultural production.
   - Increase rural incomes and improve the living standards of farming families through affordable, adaptable and proven technologies, extension and training.

3. **River Basin Development Authorities (RBDAs):**
   - Develop and manage Nigeria's surface and underground water resources.
   - Provide irrigation infrastructure and related water-management works, including flood control, to support agriculture and rural development.

4. **National Agricultural Insurance Scheme (NAIS), administered through the Nigerian Agricultural Insurance Corporation (NAIC):**
   - Protect farmers against losses to crops and livestock caused by natural hazards by providing financial support or indemnity.
   - Encourage financial institutions to provide credit to farmers and promote agricultural production.

5. **Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme Fund (ACGSF):**
   - Guarantee loans granted by banks for agricultural purposes, with the aim of increasing bank credit to the agricultural sector.
   - Reduce the risk to banks that lend to agriculture; the Central Bank of Nigeria states that the scheme guarantees 75 per cent of the net amount in default under the scheme's rules.

## Resolving the Farm Settlement Scheme Question

The Week 4 weekend question asks which programme was designed to attract young educated people to take up farming. The correct option is **B. Farm Settlement Scheme**. A historical account written by the Western Region Ministry of Agriculture describes the scheme as designed to appeal to educated young men and school leavers. Trainees attended farm institutes and were then allocated farm holdings with supervised financial support. A later appraisal identifies rural progress, viable farms operated by educated young farmers and reducing school-leaver unemployment among the scheme's objectives.

## Programme Objectives and Broad Policy Goals

Broad agricultural policy goals in the source include increasing food production, improving export-crop quality, creating employment, supplying raw materials to local industries and increasing livestock production. These are national goals.

Programme-specific objectives are narrower and linked to the programme's purpose. For example:
- Increasing water resources and irrigation infrastructure is a specific RBDA objective.
- Protecting farmers from natural hazards is a specific NAIS/NAIC objective.
- Guaranteeing agricultural bank loans is a specific ACGSF objective.
- Attracting educated young people into planned farm settlements is a specific Farm Settlement Scheme objective.

The five programmes above are examples from the programme categories named in the source. ACGSF is a named example of the agricultural loan and credit-facility category. The historical Farm Settlement Scheme is not presented as a current programme.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 5 assessment supplement: technology in agriculture
objectives: Define technology and agricultural technology in age-appropriate language.
Distinguish science from technology using agricultural examples.
Identify material and knowledge-based forms of agricultural technology.
lessons.body:
Week 5 Assessment Supplement: Technology in Agriculture

This supplement answers the Week 5 evaluation question asking for a definition of technology. It is additional teaching support, not a replacement for the original lesson.

## 1. Meaning of Technology

Technology is the practical application of knowledge to solve problems or carry out useful tasks. In agriculture, technology is the combination of tools, equipment, materials, methods and skills that farmers use to produce crops and livestock, protect resources, store produce and improve farm work.

Agricultural technology is not limited to machines. It includes both physical items and the knowledge needed to use them well.

## 2. Science and Technology

- **Science** is the systematic study of the natural world. It helps people discover and explain how things work.
- **Technology** applies knowledge from science and other experience to practical tasks. It uses tools, equipment, materials and methods to solve problems.

For example, science helps explain what nutrients plants need. Agricultural technology includes soil-testing tools, improved planting materials and farm practices that help farmers use that knowledge. Science helps explain how plants inherit traits; technology includes improved crop varieties developed through breeding.

## 3. Two Broad Types of Agricultural Technology

1. **Material technology:** physical products or materials used in farming. Examples include tools, tractors, irrigation equipment, improved seeds or plant varieties, improved animal breeds, vaccines and storage equipment.
2. **Knowledge-based technology:** information, skills and practices farmers use to manage production. Examples include crop and livestock management, crop rotation, integrated pest management, and soil and water conservation practices.

The two types work together. A farmer may have an irrigation pump (material technology), but also needs knowledge about when and how to manage water (knowledge-based technology).

## 4. Examples of Agricultural Technology

- Improved seeds and animal breeds: provide useful crop or livestock characteristics.
- Farm machinery and tools: help carry out field operations and transport materials.
- Irrigation systems: help supply water to crops when rainfall is insufficient.
- Storage structures such as silos: help protect harvested produce before use or sale.
- Crop rotation and soil-conservation practices: apply knowledge to maintain productive soil and manage crops.
- Weather, market and advisory information delivered by radio or mobile phone: helps farmers make informed decisions.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 5 assessment supplement: improved farm-management systems
objectives: Describe at least five improved farm-management systems, including crop rotation, mixed farming and rotational grazing.
Distinguish mixed farming from intercropping and crop rotation from bush fallowing.
Identify farm-management systems from simple agricultural examples.
lessons.body:
Week 5 Assessment Supplement: Improved Farm-Management Systems

A farm-management system is an organised way of using land, crops, livestock, labour and other farm resources. The systems below are examples of ways farmers can plan production and manage soil, pasture and farm resources. Their suitability depends on local soil, climate, water, labour and market conditions.

## Five Improved Farm-Management Systems

1. **Crop rotation:** Growing different crops on the same field in a planned sequence over successive seasons. A planned sequence can help maintain soil health, manage nutrients and interrupt some pest and disease cycles.
2. **Mixed farming:** Keeping crop and livestock enterprises on the same farm. Crop residues may be used as animal feed, while animal manure can be returned to crop fields; this can help reuse farm resources and spread risk.
3. **Rotational grazing:** Dividing pasture into paddocks and moving livestock between them so grazed areas can rest and regrow before animals return.
4. **Intercropping:** Growing two or more crops together in the same field during the same period. Crops may be arranged in rows or other patterns to use space and resources and reduce some production risks.
5. **Agroforestry:** Deliberately growing trees or shrubs together with crops and/or livestock on the same land-management unit. Trees can provide products such as fruit, fodder or timber and may help protect soil and water.
6. **Conservation agriculture:** Managing land around three linked principles: minimum soil disturbance, keeping the soil covered with plants or residues, and diversifying crops through rotation or association.

## Bush Fallowing: How It Differs

Bush fallowing is a traditional fallow or shifting-cultivation system. A plot is cultivated for a relatively short period and then left uncultivated for a longer period while natural vegetation regrows and the soil recovers. The farmer may cultivate another plot during the fallow period.

Bush fallowing is not the same as crop rotation:
- Crop rotation plans a sequence of different crops on the same field over successive seasons.
- Bush fallowing alternates a period of cultivation with a period when the plot is left fallow for vegetation to regrow.

Bush fallowing is also different from rotational grazing. Rotational grazing moves livestock between pasture paddocks and allows grazed areas to rest; bush fallowing rests a cultivated land plot through a fallow period. Bush fallowing is a land-use system, not simply another name for crop rotation.

## Important Distinctions

- Mixed farming combines crop and livestock enterprises; intercropping combines two or more crops in the same field.
- Rotational grazing manages livestock and pasture; crop rotation manages the sequence of crops on arable land.
- The systems are not one-size-fits-all. Farmers choose practices that suit local conditions and available resources.

Intercropping — Two or more crops are grown together in the same field during the same period. 5. Agroforestry — Trees or shrubs are deliberately integrated with crops and/or livestock. 6. Conservation agriculture — The system combines minimum soil disturbance, permanent soil cover and crop diversification.

lessons.title: Week 5 assessment supplement: modern agricultural storage facilities
objectives: Identify at least five modern agricultural storage facilities and state the produce stored in each.
Distinguish storage facilities from processing equipment such as millers, shellers and dryers.
Explain how storage structures help protect harvested produce and reduce post-harvest losses.
lessons.body:
Week 5 Assessment Supplement: Modern Agricultural Storage Facilities

An agricultural storage facility is a structure or enclosed storage system used to keep harvested produce for a period while protecting its quality and reducing losses before use, processing or sale.

## Examples of Modern Agricultural Storage Facilities

1. **Grain silo or strategic national silo:** Stores bulk dry grains such as maize, rice, wheat and sorghum. Silos are used for larger-volume or longer-term grain storage.
2. **Community warehouse:** Stores bagged grains, legumes, seeds and other durable produce until distribution or sale.
3. **Cold room:** Uses a cool, controlled environment to store perishable produce such as fruits, vegetables, dairy products, meat or fish.
4. **Improved ventilated crib:** A ventilated structure for drying and storing unthreshed grain, especially maize still on the cob.
5. **Diffuse-light store:** A storage facility used for potatoes.
6. **Improved yam barn:** Stores yams in a structure that allows the stored tubers to be monitored and helps prevent sprouting and spoilage.
7. **Cassava warehouse:** A warehouse system for storing freshly harvested cassava roots; the Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute describes a method using moist sawdust.
8. **Hermetic metal silo or drum:** A sealed storage system for grains and other dry commodities.
9. **Evaporative-cooling store:** A short-term storage structure that helps preserve fruits and vegetables where a conventional cold room is not available.

## Storage Facilities and Processing Equipment Are Different

- A **storage facility** holds produce for a period while helping to maintain its quality. Examples include a silo, warehouse, cold room, crib, yam barn and diffuse-light store.
- **Processing equipment** changes, separates or prepares produce. A miller grinds grain into flour; a sheller separates grain or kernels from cobs or pods; a dryer reduces moisture before storage. These machines may be used in the post-harvest chain, but they are not storage facilities.

The Week 5 source block 432 groups millers and shellers with storage facilities. For technical accuracy, this supplement identifies them as processing equipment and lists actual storage structures separately. The original source is not changed.

practice.question: Name five modern agricultural storage facilities and state one type of produce stored in each.
practice.answer: 1. Grain silo or strategic national silo — Bulk dry grains such as maize, rice, wheat or sorghum. 2. Community warehouse — Bagged grains, legumes, seeds and other durable produce. 3. Cold room — Perishable fruits, vegetables, dairy products, meat or fish. 4. Improved ventilated crib — Unthreshed grains, especially maize still on the cob. 5. Diffuse-light store — Potatoes.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 6 supplement: industry-provided agricultural storage structures and supply chains
objectives: Identify at least five agricultural storage structures and match each with suitable produce.
Explain how storage structures support the movement of agricultural produce from farms to processors and markets.
Select a suitable storage structure for different crops and justify the choice.
lessons.body:
Week 6 Supplement: Agricultural Storage Structures and the Supply Chain

The Week 6 source explains that industries provide storage facilities, but it does not fully match particular structures with the produce stored in them. This original supplement supplies those examples and explains why storage is important between harvesting, processing and sale. It adds teaching support; it does not rewrite the original source.

## 1. Meaning and purpose of agricultural storage

An agricultural storage structure is a building, enclosure or designed storage system used to keep harvested crops for a period before they are processed, transported, sold or used. A suitable structure helps protect produce from avoidable damage and deterioration.

Storage is an important link in the agricultural supply chain:

1. Farmers harvest crops.
2. Produce is handled and taken to a suitable storage facility.
3. The produce is kept until it is needed by a processor, trader, retailer or consumer.
4. It is then moved to processing, distribution or sale.

Good storage helps to maintain produce quality, reduce post-harvest losses and make supplies available beyond the exact time of harvest. It can also help farmers and cooperatives collect produce from different farms before sending it to a market or processing industry.

## 2. Examples of storage structures and the produce stored in them

### A. Improved inert-atmosphere silo

A silo is a large storage structure used mainly for bulk grain. An improved inert-atmosphere silo is designed for longer-term storage of dry grains. Examples of suitable produce include maize, rice, sorghum and wheat. NSPRI identifies improved inert-atmosphere silos as a technology for long-term grain storage.

### B. Improved ventilated crib

A ventilated crib is a structure that allows air to move around produce stored inside it. NSPRI identifies its improved ventilated crib for drying and storing unthreshed grains, particularly maize still on the cob. This is different from a silo that stores bulk grain after it has been separated from the cob.

### C. Improved yam barn

A yam barn is a structure used to store yam tubers after curing. Curing is the post-harvest process that allows harvested yams to develop a protective surface before storage. NSPRI explains that its improved yam-barn design allows stored yams to be monitored closely, helping to prevent sprouting and spoilage. FAO also describes the yam barn as a traditional West African structure for storing yams after curing.

### D. Cassava warehouse

A cassava warehouse is a storage system intended for freshly harvested cassava roots. NSPRI lists a cassava-warehouse technology for fresh roots. The exact storage method and period depend on the designed system and its operating conditions; learners should not assume that every ordinary warehouse can preserve fresh cassava in the same way.

### E. Cold room

A cold room is an insulated room with a controlled cool environment. It is used for perishable produce that deteriorates quickly under unsuitable conditions. Examples include many fruits and vegetables. Nigeria's Postharvest Systems Transformation Programme identifies cold rooms as part of the storage infrastructure planned for the country. A cold room is not suitable for every crop: the storage conditions must match the produce.

### F. Community warehouse

A community warehouse is a shared storage facility serving farmers, cooperatives or a local produce-trading community. It can receive bagged dry produce such as grains, legumes and seeds for aggregation, temporary storage and later distribution. The exact commodities accepted depend on the warehouse design and management. Nigeria's Postharvest Systems Transformation Programme identifies community-level warehouses and strategic national silos as parts of the national storage system.

## 3. How industries provide storage

Storage infrastructure can be provided in different ways:

- Agricultural storage companies may build and operate warehouses or cold rooms.
- Engineering and equipment businesses may supply silo systems and other storage infrastructure.
- Cooperatives and farmer groups may organise shared warehouses for members.
- Public research institutions such as NSPRI develop and demonstrate post-harvest technologies.
- Government and private organisations may work together to finance or manage storage infrastructure.

The Nigerian Government's post-harvest programme describes community-level warehouses, cold rooms and strategic national silos managed through public-private partnerships. This is an example of how public institutions and private businesses can work together to provide storage services.

A traditional yam barn is a farm-level storage structure; an improved yam barn is a developed storage technology. Not every storage structure is a factory-made machine. The important point is that suitable structures and storage services can be provided by agricultural industries, research institutions, cooperatives and public-private programmes.

## 4. Choosing a suitable storage structure

Different crops have different storage needs. Dry grains, unthreshed maize cobs, cured yams, fresh cassava roots and fresh vegetables should not automatically be placed in the same type of store.

When selecting a facility, consider the type of produce, whether it is dry or fresh, how easily it spoils, the need for ventilation or a controlled cool environment, how long it is expected to remain in storage, and whether the facility can protect it from moisture, pests and physical damage.

FAO explains that storage quality depends on factors such as temperature, relative humidity and air circulation. Produce stored together should also be compatible with the conditions in the store. Therefore, the correct facility depends on the crop and the purpose of storage.

Remember: a miller or sheller processes produce; it does not store it. A storage structure keeps produce for a period before its next stage in the supply chain.

## 5. Quick revision

- Silo — bulk dry grains such as maize, rice, sorghum and wheat.
- Improved ventilated crib — unthreshed maize, especially maize on the cob.
- Improved yam barn — cured yam tubers.
- Cassava warehouse — fresh cassava roots in a system designed for that purpose.
- Cold room — suitable perishable fruits and vegetables.
- Community warehouse — bagged grains, legumes, seeds and other accepted durable produce.

The structures are not interchangeable. A farmer, cooperative or storage operator should select a facility that suits the produce and its intended storage period.

objectives: Define a game reserve and explain its conservation purpose.
Identify at least five documented Nigerian game reserves and locate each in the correct state.
Verify the four examples in the original source, preserving the original spellings while distinguishing corrected names and present-day protected-area status.
Distinguish conservation/protected-area use from the narrower statistical category of agricultural land.
lessons.body:
Week 7 Supplement: Nigerian Game Reserves and Their Locations

## 1. What is a game reserve?

A game reserve is a protected area set aside to conserve wild animals and the habitats they depend on. It helps protect wildlife, plants, water sources and natural landscapes. The activities allowed in a reserve are controlled by the responsible authority and the rules for that protected area.

Game reserves are important for more than seeing wild animals. They can support conservation research, environmental education and carefully managed nature tourism. They also help protect habitats and biodiversity for future generations.

## 2. Five Nigerian game reserves and their locations

The following are five documented Nigerian game reserves. Learn both the name and the state in which each is located.

1. **Yankari Game Reserve — Bauchi State.** It is in north-eastern Nigeria. It is known for its savanna woodland and wildlife, including elephants and other large mammals. It is managed by the Bauchi State Government.
2. **Falgore Game Reserve — Kano State.** It is in the southern part of Kano State. The Kano State Zoological and Wildlife Management Agency identifies it as one of the facilities under its responsibility.
3. **Lame-Burra Game Reserve — Bauchi State.** It is in Lame District, Toro Local Government Area, Bauchi State.
4. **Sambisa Game Reserve — Borno State.** It is in southern Borno State, between Gwoza and Bama Local Government Areas.
5. **Kwiambana Game Reserve — Zamfara State.** A Federal Government environmental-management report identifies it in Zamfara State, where it shares an ecosystem boundary with Kamuku National Park in Kaduna State.

These examples show that game reserves occur in different parts of Nigeria. A reserve's name, legal status and management arrangements may change over time, so the responsible government authority should be consulted for current access or visitor information.

## 3. Checking the four examples in the original source

The original Week 7 notes list four places using these exact spellings: **“Kanji National Park”, “Borgu Game Reserve”, “Zurguma Game Reserve” and “Yankari Game Reserve”.** These original spellings are retained here as evidence of what the source says. The corrections below are based on the cited official records; they do not alter the original source document.

- **“Kanji National Park”** should be identified as **Kainji Lake National Park**, the official name used by the Nigeria National Park Service. The park is located in Niger and Kwara States.
- **“Borgu Game Reserve”** and **“Zurguma Game Reserve”** refer to former game reserves. The Nigeria National Park Service records that the former Borgu and **Zugurma** game reserves were amalgamated to form Kainji Lake National Park in 1976. Borgu and Zugurma are now the names of the park's two sectors, not two separate current game reserves.
- The source's spelling **“Zurguma”** differs from the official spelling **“Zugurma”** used by the Nigeria National Park Service.
- **Yankari Game Reserve** is in Bauchi State. It was upgraded to a national park in 1991 and responsibility for its management was returned to the Bauchi State Government in 2006. It is again referred to as Yankari Game Reserve.

Therefore, the original list contains four names, but it does not provide five distinct current game reserves. The corrected Kainji history also shows why Borgu and Zugurma should not be counted separately as current reserves.

## 4. Why game reserves are important

Game reserves:

- protect wild animals and the places where they live;
- help conserve biodiversity and natural habitats;
- provide places for scientific research and environmental education;
- can support tourism and income for nearby communities when tourism is properly managed; and
- help preserve natural resources for future generations.

A game reserve is a **conservation or protected-area use of land**. It is not the same as land used directly to grow crops or keep farm livestock. In the standard FAO/United Nations statistical definition, agricultural land includes arable land, permanent crops, and permanent meadows and pastures. Nature-reserve activities are classified separately. This distinction matters because the source lists wildlife conservation among agricultural uses, while its assessment also treats a game reserve as land not used for farming. Learners should understand the difference between the broad idea of land use and the narrower statistical category of agricultural land.

## 5. Quick revision

- A game reserve protects wildlife and natural habitats.
- Yankari Game Reserve is in Bauchi State.
- Falgore Game Reserve is in Kano State.
- Lame-Burra Game Reserve is in Bauchi State.
- Sambisa Game Reserve is in Borno State.
- Kwiambana Game Reserve is in Zamfara State.
- Kainji Lake National Park was formed from the former Borgu and Zugurma game reserves; it is not a separate game reserve in addition to them.

lessons.subject: Agricultural Science
lessons.title: Week 7 supplement: socio-economic factors affecting land use
objectives: Define socio-economic factors affecting land use and distinguish them from physical factors.
Explain five socio-economic factors affecting land use in Nigeria, with practical examples.
Explain how population, land tenure, economic incentives, infrastructure and government decisions can interact to change land use.
lessons.body:
Week 7 Supplement: Socio-economic Factors Affecting Land Use

## 1. Meaning of land use

Land use means the way people use an area of land. Examples include crop farming, livestock grazing, housing, markets, roads, schools, factories, forestry and wildlife conservation.

Socio-economic factors are conditions connected with people, society and the economy that influence how land is obtained, valued, shared and used. They are different from physical factors such as soil type, slope, rainfall and temperature.

Five important socio-economic factors that affect land use are explained below.

## 2. Five socio-economic factors affecting land use

### A. Population growth and urbanisation

Population growth means an increase in the number of people living in an area. As population increases, people need more food, houses, schools, hospitals, markets, roads and other services.

Urbanisation is the growth of towns and cities as more people live and work in urban areas. When a town expands, nearby farmland may be converted to residential estates, shops, roads, schools or industrial sites. At the same time, a larger population creates greater demand for food and other agricultural products.

**Example:** If a town expands towards a farming community, some farms may be converted into houses and shops. Farmers may have less land close to the town, even though the town's demand for food is increasing.

### B. Land tenure, ownership and customary practices

Land tenure refers to the rules and arrangements that determine who may occupy, control, inherit, rent or use land. In Nigeria, land may be held or used through state/public, private/family or communal arrangements, alongside statutory and customary rights.

Family customs, inheritance practices and community rules can influence who receives access to land, how land is shared and whether a farmer can continue using a plot. Secure and clear rights can encourage people to invest in improvements such as soil conservation, irrigation or farm buildings. Unclear or disputed rights can discourage long-term investment.

**Example:** A farmer who is confident that the family or community will allow continued use of a plot may be more willing to improve it. If access is uncertain, the farmer may avoid spending money on improvements that take several years to produce benefits.

### C. Income, prices, market demand and access to markets

People often choose how to use land partly by considering the income they expect to earn. Farmers may choose crops or livestock according to market demand, selling prices, production costs and the distance to buyers.

Where a crop has a reliable market and can be transported at a reasonable cost, farmers may be encouraged to use more land for it. Where input costs are high or markets are difficult to reach, some forms of farming may become less attractive. Land may instead be used for another crop, grazing, housing or a different economic activity.

**Example:** If buyers offer a reliable price for tomatoes and a road makes it easier to transport them, a farmer may decide to use part of the farm for tomato production. If transport costs become too high, the farmer may choose a crop that is easier to store or sell locally.

### D. Infrastructure and public services

Infrastructure includes facilities such as roads, bridges, electricity, water supply, drainage and communication networks. Public services include schools, health centres, markets and other facilities used by the community.

These facilities need land to be built. A new road, school, hospital, market or industrial facility may therefore change the way nearby land is used. Better roads can also make farmland easier to reach and products easier to transport. Infrastructure can support agriculture, but it can also take land away from farming when land is allocated to buildings or transport routes.

**Example:** When a road is built through a farming area, a strip of farmland may be used for the road. However, the remaining farms may become easier to reach and their produce may reach markets more quickly.

### E. Government laws, policies and land-use planning

Government decisions influence how land is allocated and what activities may take place on it. Laws and policies may provide land for agriculture, housing, roads, schools, industries, public projects or conservation. Land-use planning helps authorities and communities decide which activities are suitable for particular areas and how competing needs should be balanced.

In Nigeria, the Land Use Act of 1978 places land in each state under the Governor, to be held in trust for the people. It provides for state control and management of urban land and local-government control and management of other land, subject to the Act. The law also provides for allocation of rights of occupancy for different purposes. This means that government land decisions can influence whether land is used for farming, housing, commerce or other purposes.

**Example:** A government may allocate an area for a school, road or industrial project. The land may then change from farming to public or commercial use. A land-use plan may also protect an area for farming or conservation.

## 3. How the factors work together

Socio-economic factors often act together rather than separately.

For example, a town's population may increase. More people need houses and services. A new road may make nearby farmland more valuable. Families may decide to sell or lease some land, while government may approve new housing or commercial development. As a result, the pattern of land use changes.

The same road may also help farmers transport produce to market. Therefore, a socio-economic factor can create both opportunities and challenges for agriculture.

## 4. Socio-economic factors and physical factors

Do not confuse socio-economic factors with physical factors.

- **Socio-economic factors** arise from people, society, economic activities and institutions. Examples include population growth, land ownership, market prices, roads, public services and government policy.
- **Physical factors** arise from the natural characteristics of the land and environment. Examples include soil type, slope or topography, rainfall, temperature and water availability.

Both groups influence land use, but they are not the same.

## 5. Quick revision

1. Population growth and urbanisation increase demand for food, housing and public services and can change the amount of land available for farming.
2. Land tenure, ownership and customary practices influence who can use land and whether people feel secure enough to improve it.
3. Income, prices, market demand and market access influence which crops or other activities people choose.
4. Infrastructure and public services need land, but they can also improve access to farms and markets.
5. Government laws, policies and land-use plans influence how land is allocated and what it may be used for.

Remember: land use is influenced by both human and economic decisions and the physical characteristics of the land.

practice.question: State five socio-economic factors that affect land use and briefly explain how each can influence land use.
practice.answer: 1. Population growth and urbanisation increase demand for housing, services and food and may convert farmland to built-up areas. 2. Land tenure, ownership and customary practices determine who can access or inherit land and whether use is secure. 3. Income, prices, market demand and market access influence which crops or activities are profitable. 4. Infrastructure and public services such as roads, schools and markets require land but can also improve access to farms and buyers. 5. Government laws, policies and land-use plans influence how land is allocated for farming, housing, commerce, industry or conservation.

practice.question: Give two examples of physical factors and two examples of socio-economic factors affecting land use.
practice.answer: Physical factors: soil type and slope/topography (rainfall or temperature are also acceptable). Socio-economic factors: population growth and land tenure (income/market access, infrastructure or government policy are also acceptable).

marking.criterion: Gives two correct physical factors, one mark each.
Gives two correct socio-economic factors, one mark each.

practice.question: A town is expanding towards a farming community. A new road is built, more houses and shops are proposed, and buyers begin paying higher prices for vegetables. Identify three socio-economic factors in this situation and explain how each may affect land use.
practice.answer: Population growth/urbanisation increases demand for houses and services and may convert some farmland. Infrastructure development (the new road) takes land for transport but may also improve access to farms and markets. Market demand and prices may encourage farmers to use more land for vegetables because the expected income is higher.

marking.criterion: Identifies population growth/urbanisation and explains the pressure for housing or services.
Identifies infrastructure development and explains its land requirement or improved access.
Identifies market demand/prices and explains how they influence crop or land-use choices.

practice.question: Explain two ways in which land tenure and government policy can influence land use.
practice.answer: Land tenure determines who can occupy, inherit, rent or use land and how secure that access is. Secure rights may encourage long-term farm improvements, while uncertain or disputed access can discourage investment. Government laws and policies influence who allocates land and which purposes may be approved, such as agriculture, housing, roads, commerce or conservation.

Explains how government laws, allocation decisions or land-use plans influence permitted or planned uses.
