lessons.body:
# Third Term, Week Two: Farm Power — Matching Power Sources to Farm Operations

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. Explain farm power and distinguish a power source from the machine or implement it drives.
2. Identify farm operations that use mechanical, electrical, wind and solar power.
3. Give at least two accurate farm-operation examples for each of the four power sources.
4. Explain the difference between a solar photovoltaic pump and a solar-thermal crop dryer.
5. Select a suitable power source for a farm task and state relevant limitations and safety precautions.

## 1. Meaning of farm power

Farm power is the energy or force used to carry out work on a farm. It enables a farmer to prepare land, plant crops, irrigate, care for livestock, harvest, process and transport produce.

A **power source** supplies the energy. A **machine or implement** receives or uses that energy. The **farm operation** is the job being done.

For example:

- Power source: mechanical power from a diesel engine.
- Machine: tractor pulling a plough.
- Farm operation: primary tillage, which cuts and turns the soil.

Do not confuse the machine with the power source. A tractor is a machine; its engine supplies mechanical power. A water pump is a machine; it may be driven by an electric motor, a diesel engine, a windmill or a solar-powered motor.

## 2. Mechanical power

Mechanical power on a farm is commonly supplied by an engine, such as a petrol or diesel engine. The engine produces motion that can drive a machine directly or through a transmission system. A tractor may pull an implement using its drawbar or drive suitable equipment through a power take-off (PTO).

### Farm operations using mechanical power

| Operation | Machine or equipment | How mechanical power is used |
|---|---|---|
| Land preparation | Tractor with plough | The tractor pulls the plough through the soil to cut and turn it. |
| Secondary tillage | Tractor with harrow | The tractor pulls the harrow to break soil clods and prepare a finer seedbed. |
| Ridging | Tractor with ridger | The tractor pulls the ridger to form ridges for crops that require them. |
| Planting or sowing | Tractor-mounted or tractor-drawn planter/seed drill | The tractor moves and powers the implement that places seed at the required spacing and depth. |
| Harvesting | Combine harvester or tractor-powered harvesting equipment | The engine powers cutting, threshing and crop-handling mechanisms. |
| Post-harvest processing | Engine-driven thresher, sheller or mill | The engine drives rotating or reciprocating parts that separate grain or process produce. |

**Two clear examples for the assessment:** (1) a tractor pulling a plough to prepare land; and (2) an engine-driven thresher separating grain after harvest. Other valid examples include harrowing, ridging, mechanised planting, harvesting and milling.

The National Agricultural Extension and Research Liaison Services (NAERLS) identifies tractor services for land clearing, ploughing, harrowing and ridging, and also works with planters, threshers/shellers and dryers. The exact machine selected depends on the crop, field conditions, farm size and available service support.

## 3. Electrical power

Electrical power is energy supplied through an electrical system, such as the public grid, a generator or a suitable renewable-electricity system. An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical motion. Other electrical equipment converts it into heat, light, cooling or controlled movement.

### Farm operations using electrical power

| Operation | Electrical equipment | How electricity helps |
|---|---|---|
| Irrigation and water supply | Electric water pump | An electric motor drives a pump that lifts or moves water through pipes or channels to the farm. |
| Milking | Milking machine | An electric motor and vacuum system operate equipment used to extract milk hygienically. |
| Brooding | Electric brooder or heating equipment | Electricity supplies controlled heat to help maintain suitable conditions for young chicks. |
| Crop and livestock-product processing | Electric motor driving a grinder, sheller, mixer or conveyor | The motor supplies motion to process feed or agricultural produce. |
| Storage and preservation | Refrigerator or cold room | Electrical refrigeration removes heat and helps maintain a suitable storage temperature. |
| Ventilation | Electric fans | Fans move air in poultry houses, greenhouses or storage areas where ventilation is required. |

**Two clear examples for the assessment:** (1) operating an electric pump to supply irrigation water; and (2) operating a milking machine. Brooder heating, feed grinding, shelling, refrigeration and ventilation are additional examples.

Nigeria's National Board for Technical Education curriculum specifically identifies brooder-pen heating, milking equipment, irrigation pumping and processing machines as farm uses of electricity.

### Electrical safety

Electricity can cause electric shock, burns and fire. Farm electrical installations and repairs must be handled by a qualified electrician. Keep electrical connections protected from water, use suitable earthing and circuit protection, keep cables away from animals and machinery, and never touch switches or equipment with wet hands. Disconnect and isolate equipment before cleaning or servicing it.

## 4. Wind power

Wind power is energy from moving air. A windmill can convert wind movement into mechanical motion. A wind turbine converts wind movement into electricity.

### Farm operations using wind power

| Operation | Equipment | How wind power is used |
|---|---|---|
| Lifting water | Windmill or windpump | Wind turns the blades; a mechanical linkage drives a pump that raises water from a well or other suitable source. The water may be stored for livestock or irrigation. |
| Grinding grain | Traditional windmill and millstones | Wind turns the sails and drive shaft, which turns millstones to grind grain. |
| Winnowing | Natural wind or a wind-assisted winnower | Moving air separates lighter chaff from heavier grain. A manually operated winnower is not automatically a wind-powered machine; the source of the airflow must be identified. |
| Drying produce | Sun and moving air, or a wind-assisted drying arrangement | Air movement helps moisture leave produce. This may use natural wind rather than a windmill, so do not describe every open-air drying activity as mechanically powered by a windmill. |

**Two clear examples for the assessment:** (1) using a windpump to lift water for livestock or irrigation; and (2) using a windmill to drive a grain mill. These are established mechanical uses of windmills.

Wind is not constant. A windpump or windmill works best at a site with a suitable and sufficiently reliable wind resource. A farm may need water storage or a backup pump for periods when the wind is weak.

## 5. Solar power

Solar power is energy from sunlight. Farms can use it in two main ways:

- **Solar photovoltaic (PV) systems** convert sunlight into electricity. The electricity can operate a pump, fan, light or other suitable electrical equipment.
- **Solar-thermal systems** capture the sun's heat directly. A solar crop dryer uses this heat to warm air and remove moisture from produce.

### Farm operations using solar power

| Operation | Solar equipment | How solar energy is used |
|---|---|---|
| Irrigation and water supply | Solar PV water-pumping system | Solar panels generate electricity for a motor that drives a water pump. The water is delivered to a storage tank or irrigation system. |
| Crop drying | Solar crop dryer | Sunlight heats the drying chamber or air collector. Warm air passes around produce and removes moisture. |
| Crop and livestock-product preservation | Solar-assisted dryer or hybrid dryer | Solar heat provides drying energy; some systems use a PV-powered fan to move air through the drying chamber. |
| Farm lighting or small equipment | Solar PV panels, charge controller and battery/inverter where required | Solar electricity can supply suitable lights and small electrical loads. The system must be correctly sized for the equipment. |

**Two clear examples for the assessment:** (1) using solar panels to power a water pump for irrigation; and (2) drying suitable crops in a solar dryer. These are different uses of solar energy: the first uses photovoltaic electricity, while the second uses solar heat.

A World Bank case study describes solar-powered pumps being used by a farmer in Niger to irrigate fields and diversify crops. In Nigeria, FAO reported solar-powered tomato-drying centres and solar-powered pumps in a Kaduna State project. The Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute also provides guidance on operating solar dryers safely and hygienically.

## 6. Compare the four power sources

| Power source | Two or more farm operations | Main equipment | Important limitation or condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mechanical | Ploughing; threshing; planting; harvesting | Tractor, plough, planter, thresher or engine-driven mill | Requires capital, fuel or energy supply, maintenance and trained operators. |
| Electrical | Irrigation pumping; milking; brooding; feed grinding | Electric pump, milking machine, brooder, motor-driven grinder | Needs a safe and dependable electrical supply; shock and fire hazards must be controlled. |
| Wind | Water pumping; grain milling | Windpump or windmill | Depends on a suitable wind site and sufficiently reliable wind. |
| Solar | Water pumping; crop drying | Solar PV pump; solar-thermal dryer | Output varies with sunlight, weather, system design and storage; equipment has an initial cost. |

## 7. Choosing the right power source

A farmer should not select a power source only because it is modern or renewable. The choice should fit the operation and local conditions.

Consider:

1. **The operation:** Is the task ploughing, pumping water, milking, drying or grinding?
2. **The required power:** How much work must be done, and how quickly?
3. **The site:** Is there a reliable electrical connection, suitable wind, adequate sunlight or a suitable water source?
4. **The scale:** Is the system suitable for a small plot, a medium-sized farm or a large commercial operation?
5. **The cost:** Consider purchase, installation, fuel or electricity, repairs and replacement parts.
6. **Maintenance and skills:** Are spare parts, trained operators and repair services available?
7. **Safety and the environment:** Can the equipment be operated safely without unacceptable pollution, noise, soil damage or risks to people and animals?

### Worked examples

**Example A — A farm needs to lift water and has a suitable windy site but no grid connection.** A windpump may be appropriate if wind measurements and water needs justify it. A solar pump or engine-driven pump may be considered as an alternative or backup. The decision depends on the site and the cost of maintaining the system.

**Example B — A tomato cooperative wants to dry produce while protecting it from dust, insects and rain.** A suitable solar dryer can use sunlight to heat air in a protected chamber. Trays, airflow, loading depth and cooling before packaging affect the quality of the dried produce. A solar dryer is not the same as a solar-powered irrigation pump.

**Example C — A dairy farm needs to milk several cows.** A properly installed electric milking machine can reduce manual effort and support regular milking. The farm must provide safe electricity, clean equipment, maintenance and hygienic milk handling.

**Example D — A farmer must prepare a large field for planting within a short period.** A tractor with a suitable plough, harrow or ridger can carry out the relevant land-preparation operations. The implement must match the soil and operation; a tractor alone does not perform every task.

## 8. Important distinctions and source limitations

- A tractor is a machine; mechanical power from its engine drives or pulls implements.
- A pump is a machine, not a power source. It may be driven by an electric motor, diesel engine, windmill or solar-powered motor.
- A solar PV pump uses electricity generated by solar panels. A solar-thermal dryer uses heat from sunlight. They are not the same technology.
- A windmill that drives a grain mill or pump supplies mechanical power. A modern wind turbine that drives a generator supplies electricity.
- Water used for irrigation, washing produce or seed germination is a farm resource. It is not automatically hydropower. Hydropower specifically involves energy captured from moving or falling water to drive a turbine or waterwheel.
- The original Week Two weekend question asking for the “most common” grain-drying power source in West Africa is not answered by the source's examples. Solar drying and wind-assisted drying are both mentioned, but that does not establish regional prevalence. Do not guess an answer from the examples; the separate regional fact-check remains open.

## 9. Safety reminders

- Operate tractors, harvesters and engine-driven machines only after proper instruction. Keep guards in place and stay away from moving belts, shafts and PTO parts.
- Never refuel a hot engine. Keep fuel away from flames and provide ventilation to prevent exhaust-gas exposure.
- Do not attempt electrical wiring or repairs without a qualified electrician. Isolate equipment before cleaning or maintenance.
- Keep people away from moving windmill blades, shafts and pump linkages. Do not climb a windmill tower.
- Install and maintain solar panels, batteries, controllers and pumps according to the manufacturer's instructions. Protect electrical components from water and accidental contact.
- Never bypass a safety guard or operate equipment with a damaged cable, exposed wire or loose moving part.

## 10. Check your understanding

### Question 1 (4 marks)
Define farm power and explain the difference between a power source and a farm machine.

**Answer:** Farm power is the energy or force used to carry out work on a farm. A power source supplies energy, while a machine uses or converts that energy to perform a task. For example, electricity is the source, an electric pump is the machine, and irrigation pumping is the operation.

**Marking:** 2 marks for a correct definition; 1 mark for explaining a power source; 1 mark for explaining a machine with a suitable example.

### Question 2 (4 marks)
State two farm operations that use mechanical power and name the machine used for each.

**Answer:** Tractor ploughing for land preparation; engine-driven threshing to separate grain. Other valid answers include harrowing, ridging, mechanised planting, combine harvesting and engine-driven milling.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each valid operation and 1 mark for the matching machine, up to 4.

### Question 3 (4 marks)
State two farm operations that use electrical power and name the equipment used.

**Answer:** Pumping water for irrigation using an electric pump; milking using an electric milking machine. Other valid examples include brooder heating, electric feed grinding, refrigeration and ventilation fans.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each valid operation and 1 mark for the matching electrical equipment, up to 4.

### Question 4 (4 marks)
State two farm operations that can be performed using wind power and explain how wind supplies the energy.

**Answer:** A windpump can lift water for irrigation or livestock; a windmill can drive millstones to grind grain. Wind turns the blades or sails, which transfer motion through a shaft or linkage to the pump or mill.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each correct operation; 1 mark for explaining the wind-to-machine motion; 1 mark for correctly connecting the motion to the pump or mill.

### Question 5 (4 marks)
State two farm operations that use solar power and distinguish how solar energy is used in each.

**Answer:** A solar PV system generates electricity to drive an irrigation pump. A solar-thermal dryer captures sunlight as heat to warm air and dry crops.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each correct operation; 1 mark for correctly explaining the PV/electricity use; 1 mark for correctly explaining direct solar heat in drying.

### Question 6 (4 marks)
Explain the difference between a windmill and a wind turbine.

**Answer:** A windmill uses wind to provide mechanical motion directly, for example to pump water or grind grain. A wind turbine uses wind to drive a generator and produce electricity.

**Marking:** 2 marks for the windmill explanation; 2 marks for the wind-turbine explanation.

### Question 7 (8 marks)
Match each operation to the most suitable power source from mechanical, electrical, wind or solar:
a. A tractor pulls a plough to turn the soil.
b. An electric motor drives a milking machine.
c. A windpump raises water from a well.
d. A solar dryer warms air to dry tomatoes.
e. A tractor-powered thresher separates grain.
f. A solar PV pump supplies irrigation water.
g. A windmill turns millstones to grind grain.
h. An electric pump moves water through irrigation pipes.

**Answer:** a. Mechanical; b. Electrical; c. Wind; d. Solar; e. Mechanical; f. Solar; g. Wind; h. Electrical.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each correct source.

### Question 8 (8 marks)
A farmer in a remote area wants to pump water for irrigation. The site has a suitable wind resource and good sunlight, but no grid connection. The farmer also belongs to a cooperative that wants to dry tomatoes. Recommend a suitable power source and equipment for each task. Give two factors the farmer should consider before choosing the equipment.

**Answer:** For irrigation, the farmer could compare a windpump with a solar PV water-pumping system. A windpump uses wind to drive a pump; a solar PV system uses panels to generate electricity for a pump. For the cooperative's tomatoes, a suitable solar dryer can use sunlight as heat to dry the produce in a protected chamber. Factors include local wind and sunlight availability, water demand, equipment and installation cost, maintenance and spare parts, storage/backup requirements, and operator skills.

**Marking:** 2 marks for a suitable wind or solar pumping option and explanation; 2 marks for identifying a suitable solar dryer for tomatoes; 2 marks for two relevant selection factors; 2 marks for explaining how the chosen equipment matches the operation and local conditions.

**Total: 40 marks.** Each question's marking criteria add up to its stated marks.

## References

1. National Agricultural Extension and Research Liaison Services (NAERLS), Agricultural Engineering and Irrigation: https://naerls.gov.ng/agric-engineering-and-irrigation/ — Nigerian examples of tractor land preparation and agricultural equipment development.
2. National Board for Technical Education, Curriculum and Course Specifications for National Diploma in Agricultural Technology, Farm Electrification section: https://www.digitalnbte.nbte.gov.ng/Public/DownloadCurriculum/O4bbef40d1ae6284e8ff4d900dd401306.pdf — brooder heating, milking equipment, irrigation pumping and processing machines.
3. National Geographic Society, Putting Wind to Work: https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/putting-wind-work/4th-grade/ — windmills used to grind grain and pump water; windpumps.
4. World Bank, Solar energy brings water to Niger's farms (16 March 2023): https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/feature/2023/03/16/solar-energy-brings-water-to-niger-farms — solar-powered irrigation pumping.
5. FAO Nigeria, Solar-powered tomato drying centres in Kaduna State (9 February 2026): https://www.fao.org/nigeria/news/detail/fao-distributes-inputs-and-assets-to-end-ground-sun-drying--boost-tomato-value-chain-in-kaduna-state/en — Nigerian example of solar drying and solar water pumping.
6. Nigerian Stored Products Research Institute, Operation and Management of Solar Dryers (17 July 2026): https://postharvestblog.nspri.gov.ng/post/operation-and-management-of-solar-dryers/ — safe and hygienic solar-dryer operation.
7. Sokoto Energy Research Centre, Solar Thermal Technologies: https://serc.energy.gov.ng/pages/research/solar-thermal.html — Nigerian example of hybrid solar drying with photovoltaic-powered air blowers.

The source's original examples remain distinguishable from the additional verified examples in this supplement. No third-party image or text is reproduced. The separate regional grain-drying prevalence question, source corrections and source-image rights issues remain open for their own tasks.

lessons.body:
# Third Term, Week Four Supplement: Digestive Secretions, Shared Digestion, Blood Composition and Sphincters

This supplement teaches four concepts required by the Week Four assessments but not fully explained in the original source. It is additional teaching, not a replacement for the source's ruminant, non-ruminant, poultry, circulatory or reproductive-system lessons.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this supplement, you should be able to:

1. Distinguish bile from digestive enzymes and explain the liver's digestive role.
2. State accurate similarities between monogastric and polygastric digestion.
3. Describe the main components of blood and explain why water is a major constituent.
4. Define a sphincter and explain its role in controlling movement through the digestive tract.

## 1. The liver, bile and digestive enzymes

The liver is an important accessory organ of digestion. It produces **bile**, a digestive secretion that helps the body digest and absorb fats. The liver does not supply a digestive enzyme called a liver enzyme to the intestinal lumen in the way the pancreas supplies pancreatic enzymes.

### What is bile?

Bile is a fluid made by the liver. In animals that have a gallbladder, the gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals and releases it into the duodenum when needed. In some animal species, bile flows from the liver to the intestine without being stored in a gallbladder.

Bile contains bile salts (bile acids), water and other substances. Bile salts help to **emulsify fats**. Emulsification breaks large fat globules into many smaller droplets. This increases the surface area on which the enzyme lipase can act. Bile therefore assists fat digestion, but bile itself is **not a digestive enzyme**.

Bile also helps the absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

### Bile compared with enzymes

| Feature | Bile | Digestive enzymes |
|---|---|---|
| Main source | Made by the liver | Made by digestive glands such as the salivary glands, stomach, pancreas and small-intestinal lining |
| Is it an enzyme? | No | Yes; enzymes speed up specific chemical reactions |
| Main role | Bile salts emulsify fats and help fat absorption | Break large food molecules into smaller molecules that can be absorbed |
| Example | Bile salts help disperse fat droplets | Lipase breaks down fats; amylase acts on starch; proteases act on proteins |

**Important distinction:** the liver produces bile, while the pancreas produces enzymes such as pancreatic lipase, amylase and proteases. The liver performs many metabolic functions and contains enzymes inside its cells, but these are not the digestive enzymes referred to in the Week Four assessment.

### Simple sequence of fat digestion

1. Food containing fat leaves the stomach and enters the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
2. Bile enters the duodenum and bile salts help disperse large fat globules into smaller droplets.
3. Pancreatic lipase acts on the fat at the increased surface area.
4. The products of fat digestion are absorbed through the intestinal lining, with bile salts also helping the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins.

## 2. Similarities between monogastric and polygastric digestion

A **monogastric** animal has one main stomach compartment. Examples include pigs. A **polygastric** animal, such as cattle, has a specialised multi-compartment stomach with rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.

Their stomach arrangements and use of fibrous feed differ, but both groups share important digestive processes.

### Similarities

1. **Ingestion through the mouth:** both take in feed through the mouth. Teeth and jaw movements help reduce feed particle size.
2. **Saliva and swallowing:** both produce saliva, which moistens feed and helps swallowing. Saliva also has other digestive and protective functions.
3. **Movement through the oesophagus:** swallowed feed moves through the oesophagus by muscular contractions called peristalsis.
4. **Stomach processing:** both have stomach regions that store, mix and process feed. The ruminant abomasum is the glandular or true stomach; the pig has a single main stomach.
5. **Chemical digestion:** both use digestive secretions and enzymes to break food components into smaller substances.
6. **Small-intestinal digestion and absorption:** both use pancreatic and intestinal enzymes in the small intestine, and most absorbable nutrients pass through the intestinal wall into the blood or lymph.
7. **Large-intestinal functions:** both have a large intestine that absorbs water and electrolytes and helps form and move faeces.
8. **Accessory organs:** both use the liver and pancreas in digestion. The liver supplies bile; the pancreas supplies digestive enzymes and other secretions.

### Why they are not identical

- Ruminants depend heavily on microbial fermentation in the rumen and other forestomach compartments to use fibrous plant materials.
- Monogastrics do not have a rumen. However, some monogastric herbivores, such as horses and rabbits, have important microbial fermentation in the caecum and large intestine.
- The pig's single stomach and the cow's four-compartment stomach are not interchangeable. The type of feed and the animal's digestive adaptations influence how feed is processed.

Do not write that bacteria help only polygastric animals. Microorganisms are present in the digestive tracts of many animals; their location and contribution to digestion differ among species.

### Comparison table

| Feature | Monogastric example: pig | Polygastric example: cattle | Similarity or difference? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mouth, teeth and saliva | Present | Present | Similar |
| Oesophagus | Present | Present | Similar |
| Main stomach arrangement | One main stomach | Four compartments: rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum | Different |
| Enzymatic digestion | Occurs in stomach and small intestine | Occurs in the abomasum and small intestine | Similar process, different stomach arrangement |
| Microbial fermentation | Occurs to a more limited extent in the hindgut than in ruminants; amount varies | Extensive fermentation occurs mainly in the rumen | Different in degree and location |
| Small intestine | Digestion and nutrient absorption | Digestion and nutrient absorption | Similar |
| Large intestine | Absorbs water; microbial activity may occur | Absorbs water; some microbial activity occurs | Similar function, varying contribution |
| Liver and pancreas | Present | Present | Similar accessory organs |

## 3. Blood composition: why water is a major constituent

Blood is a fluid connective tissue that moves through blood vessels. It transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and waste products, helps regulate body conditions and protects the animal against disease and blood loss.

Blood has two broad components:

- **Plasma:** the liquid part of blood. It contains mostly water, together with proteins, dissolved salts (electrolytes), nutrients, hormones, gases and waste products.
- **Formed elements:** the cellular components suspended in plasma. These are red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets (called thrombocytes in veterinary contexts).

### Main components and functions

| Component | Main function |
|---|---|
| Plasma | Carries dissolved substances, distributes heat, helps maintain fluid balance and transports hormones and waste products |
| Red blood cells (erythrocytes) | Carry oxygen using haemoglobin; they also help transport some carbon dioxide |
| White blood cells (leukocytes) | Defend the body against infection and foreign substances |
| Platelets or thrombocytes | Help start blood clotting and reduce blood loss after injury |

### Why water is a major constituent

Water is the largest component of plasma. In standard human physiology references, plasma is about 90–92% water; veterinary references also describe plasma as predominantly water. The exact proportions of plasma and formed elements vary with species, age, hydration, health and physiological condition, so one fixed percentage should not be applied to every farm animal.

Water in plasma acts as a solvent and transport medium. It carries dissolved nutrients, salts, hormones and waste products around the body. It also helps distribute heat and maintain blood volume.

A simple school-level description is:

**Blood = plasma + formed elements.**

Plasma contains mostly water and dissolved substances. The formed elements are red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

Do not say that the whole of blood is 90% water. The 90–92% figure refers to the water content of plasma in commonly cited human physiology references, not to a universal percentage for whole blood in every animal.

## 4. Sphincters in the digestive tract

A **sphincter** is a ring or circular band of muscle around an opening or passage. When it contracts, it narrows or closes the passage. When it relaxes, the passage opens and material can move through it.

Sphincters help control the direction and timing of movement through the digestive tract. They can also help prevent material from flowing backwards.

### Examples of digestive sphincters

| Sphincter | Location | Main function |
|---|---|---|
| Upper oesophageal sphincter | Between the pharynx and oesophagus | Opens during swallowing to allow food to enter the oesophagus |
| Lower oesophageal (cardiac/gastro-oesophageal) sphincter | Between the oesophagus and stomach | Allows swallowed food to enter the stomach and helps prevent stomach contents from moving backwards into the oesophagus |
| Pyloric sphincter | Between the stomach and duodenum | Regulates the passage of stomach contents into the small intestine |
| Ileocecal sphincter or valve | Between the ileum and caecum | Regulates movement from the small intestine into the large intestine and helps limit backflow |
| Anal sphincters | Around the anal canal | Control the release of faeces |

The sphincter of Oddi is another example. It controls the entry of bile and pancreatic secretions into the duodenum. The exact anatomical arrangement can vary among species.

### How a sphincter works: the pyloric example

1. Food is mixed with gastric juice in the stomach to form a semi-liquid material called chyme.
2. The pyloric sphincter regulates the release of small amounts of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.
3. It helps control the rate at which stomach contents enter the small intestine.
4. Its muscle tone also helps limit backward movement of intestinal contents into the stomach.

A sphincter is therefore not a separate digestive organ that produces an enzyme. It is a muscular control structure that regulates passage through a particular opening.

## 5. Quick revision

- The liver produces bile; bile is not a digestive enzyme.
- Bile salts emulsify fats and help the absorption of fats and fat-soluble vitamins.
- Pancreatic lipase is an enzyme that digests fats.
- Monogastric and polygastric animals both ingest, move, digest and absorb feed, but their stomach structures and microbial fermentation differ.
- Blood consists of plasma and formed elements. Plasma contains mostly water and dissolved substances.
- Red blood cells transport oxygen, white blood cells defend the body, and platelets help blood clot.
- A sphincter is a circular muscle that controls the opening and closing of a passage.
- Examples include the lower oesophageal, pyloric, ileocecal and anal sphincters.

## 6. Check your understanding

### Question 1 (6 marks)
Distinguish between bile and a digestive enzyme. State the role of bile in fat digestion and give one example of a digestive enzyme.

**Answer:** Bile is a fluid made by the liver; it is not an enzyme. Bile salts emulsify fats into small droplets, increasing the surface area for lipase to act and helping fat absorption. Lipase is an example of a digestive enzyme.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — States that bile is produced by the liver and is not a digestive enzyme.
- 2 marks — Explains that bile salts emulsify fats and help lipase action/absorption.
- 2 marks — Gives a correct digestive enzyme, such as lipase, amylase or a protease.

### Question 2 (8 marks)
State four similarities between monogastric and polygastric digestion and explain each briefly.

**Answer:** Both take in feed through the mouth and use chewing and saliva; both move swallowed feed through the oesophagus by peristalsis; both use chemical digestion by enzymes; both have a small intestine where nutrients are digested and absorbed; both have a large intestine that absorbs water and helps form faeces; both use the liver and pancreas as accessory digestive organs.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Gives two valid similarities.
- 2 marks — Gives two further valid similarities.
- 4 marks — Briefly explains four similarities, one mark each. Accept equivalent accurate examples.

### Question 3 (8 marks)
Name the two broad components of blood. Describe the main function of plasma, red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

**Answer:** The two broad components are plasma and formed elements. Plasma transports dissolved substances and helps maintain fluid balance. Red blood cells carry oxygen using haemoglobin. White blood cells defend the body against infection. Platelets help blood clot and reduce blood loss.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Names plasma and formed elements.
- 2 marks — Gives the function of plasma.
- 1 mark — Gives the function of red blood cells.
- 1 mark — Gives the function of white blood cells.
- 2 marks — Gives the function of platelets.

### Question 4 (6 marks)
Explain why water is described as a major constituent of blood.

**Answer:** Blood plasma contains mostly water. Water acts as a solvent and transport medium for dissolved nutrients, salts, hormones and waste products. It also helps distribute heat and maintain blood volume. The water percentage commonly quoted for plasma must not be confused with the percentage of water in whole blood.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — States that plasma is the liquid component and contains mostly water.
- 2 marks — Explains transport/solvent function.
- 1 mark — Gives another function such as heat distribution or maintaining blood volume.
- 1 mark — Distinguishes plasma water percentage from whole-blood percentage or notes species variation.

### Question 5 (6 marks)
Define a sphincter and explain the functions of the lower oesophageal, pyloric and anal sphincters.

**Answer:** A sphincter is a circular band of muscle that controls an opening or passage by contracting and relaxing. The lower oesophageal sphincter controls passage from the oesophagus into the stomach and helps prevent reflux. The pyloric sphincter controls passage from the stomach into the duodenum. The anal sphincters control the release of faeces.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Correct definition of a sphincter.
- 1 mark — Function of the lower oesophageal sphincter.
- 1 mark — Function of the pyloric sphincter.
- 2 marks — Function of the anal sphincters.

### Question 6 (6 marks)
A student says, “The liver produces an enzyme called bile, and only polygastric animals use bacteria to digest food.” Identify and correct the two errors.

**Answer:** First, bile is not an enzyme. The liver produces bile, whose bile salts emulsify fats and help fat absorption; pancreatic lipase is an enzyme that digests fats. Second, microbial activity is not exclusive to polygastric animals. Ruminants depend heavily on microbial fermentation in the rumen, but some monogastric animals, including horses and rabbits, also have important microbial fermentation in the hindgut.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Corrects the bile/enzyme error and identifies bile's function.
- 2 marks — States that ruminants have major rumen microbial fermentation.
- 2 marks — Gives an accurate monogastric hindgut-fermentation example and explains the distinction.

**Total: 40 marks.** Every marking guide adds up to the marks available for its question.

## References

1. Merck Veterinary Manual, Gallbladder, Cystic Duct, and Common Bile Duct in Animals: https://www.merckvetmanual.com/digestive-system/liver-structure-and-function/gallbladder-cystic-duct-and-common-bile-duct-in-animals — bile storage, delivery and fat digestion.
2. OpenStax Biology 2e, Components of the Blood: https://openstax.org/books/biology/pages/40-2-components-of-the-blood — plasma, formed elements and the water-rich composition of plasma.
3. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, The Mouth, Pharynx, and Esophagus: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology/pages/23-3-the-mouth-pharynx-and-esophagus — sphincters and control of passage into the oesophagus and stomach.
4. OpenStax Biology 2e, Digestive Systems: https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/34-1-digestive-systems — digestive processes, pyloric sphincter and bile versus pancreatic enzymes.
5. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, The Small and Large Intestines: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology/pages/23-5-the-small-and-large-intestines — ileocecal and anal sphincters and intestinal function.
6. Merck Veterinary Manual, The Ruminant Digestive System: https://www.merckvetmanual.com/pharmacology/systemic-pharmacotherapeutics-of-the-digestive-system/the-ruminant-digestive-system — microbial fermentation in ruminants and comparison with other mammals.
7. University of Minnesota, Vet Med: Applied GI Physiology, Monogastric Digestion: https://open.lib.umn.edu/vetphysioapplied/chapter/normal-digestion/ — digestion in monogastrics and hindgut microbial fermentation in horses and rabbits.
8. Mississippi State University Extension, Understanding the Ruminant Animal Digestive System: https://extension.msstate.edu/publications/understanding-the-ruminant-animal-digestive-system — ruminant anatomy, accessory organs, bile and nutrient absorption.
9. National Open University of Nigeria, NSC 222 Human Physiology II, sphincters section: https://nou.edu.ng/coursewarecontent/NSC%20222%20Human%20Physiology%20II.pdf — types and functions of digestive sphincters.

lessons.body:
# Third Term, Week Five Supplement: Breathing, Respiration, Neurons and Reflex Actions

This supplement adds the details needed to answer the Week Five questions on breathing mechanics, respiration in a named farm animal, the neuron and reflex action. It does not silently alter the original respiration equations or reuse the source's unlicensed figures.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. Explain how inhalation and exhalation occur in a mammal.
2. Trace air movement and gas exchange in a named farm animal.
3. Distinguish breathing, gas exchange and cellular respiration.
4. Identify the neuron as the basic structural and functional unit of nervous tissue and label its main parts.
5. Explain a reflex arc and give at least four examples of reflex action in animals.

## 1. Breathing and respiration are related but different

- **Breathing (pulmonary ventilation)** is the movement of air into and out of the lungs.
- **Gas exchange** is the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air in the lungs and the blood, and between blood and body tissues.
- **Cellular respiration** is the process by which cells release usable energy from nutrients. In aerobic respiration, cells use oxygen and produce carbon dioxide and water.

Breathing brings oxygen into the lungs and removes carbon dioxide. It supports cellular respiration, but breathing itself is not the same process as cellular respiration.

## 2. Mechanics of inhalation and exhalation in a mammal

A cow, goat, sheep and pig are mammals. Their lungs are ventilated by changes in the volume of the chest cavity and the pressure inside the lungs.

### A. Inhalation (inspiration)

1. The diaphragm contracts and moves downwards, becoming flatter.
2. The external intercostal muscles between the ribs contract and move the ribs upwards and outwards.
3. The volume of the thoracic (chest) cavity increases.
4. The lungs expand with the chest wall, so pressure inside the alveoli falls below atmospheric pressure.
5. Air moves from the atmosphere through the air passages into the lungs because it moves down a pressure gradient.

**Remember:** during inhalation, chest-cavity volume increases and pressure inside the lungs decreases, so air enters.

### B. Exhalation (expiration) during quiet breathing

1. The diaphragm relaxes and returns towards its dome-shaped position.
2. The external intercostal muscles relax and the ribs return towards their resting position.
3. Elastic recoil of the lungs and chest wall reduces the volume of the thoracic cavity.
4. Pressure inside the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure.
5. Air flows out of the lungs.

Quiet exhalation is mainly passive. During forced exhalation, such as vigorous exercise or coughing, additional muscles including the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles can help push air out.

### Comparison

| Inhalation | Exhalation during quiet breathing |
|---|---|
| Diaphragm contracts and flattens | Diaphragm relaxes and becomes dome-shaped |
| External intercostal muscles contract | External intercostal muscles relax |
| Ribs move up and out | Ribs return down and in |
| Thoracic volume increases | Thoracic volume decreases |
| Lung pressure falls below atmospheric pressure | Lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure |
| Air enters the lungs | Air leaves the lungs |

## 3. Respiration in a named farm animal: the cow

The cow is a useful example of a farm mammal with lungs. The respiratory process includes air movement, gas exchange, transport of gases in the blood and cellular respiration.

### A. Route taken by inhaled air

Air follows this general route:

**Nostrils → nasal passages → pharynx → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli**

- The nostrils and nasal passages admit, warm, moisten and filter inhaled air.
- The pharynx and larynx form the passage towards the trachea.
- The trachea carries air towards the chest and divides into two main bronchi.
- The bronchi branch into smaller bronchioles within the lungs.
- The bronchioles lead to microscopic air spaces called alveoli.

### B. Gas exchange in the lungs

Alveoli have very thin walls and are surrounded by tiny blood capillaries.

1. Oxygen concentration is higher in the air inside the alveoli than in the blood arriving at the lung capillaries.
2. Oxygen diffuses across the thin alveolar-capillary surface into the blood.
3. Much of the oxygen binds to haemoglobin inside red blood cells.
4. Carbon dioxide carried by the blood diffuses from the capillaries into the alveoli.
5. Carbon dioxide leaves the lungs when the cow exhales.

### C. Transport of gases and cellular respiration

1. Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to body tissues.
2. Oxygen moves from the blood into body cells.
3. Cells use oxygen during aerobic cellular respiration to release energy from glucose.
4. Carbon dioxide and water are produced. The carbon dioxide enters the blood and is transported back to the lungs.
5. The cow exhales the carbon dioxide.

The simplified word equation for aerobic cellular respiration is:

**Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy (ATP)**

This is a new, correctly written word equation for this supplement. It is not a replacement or silent correction of the unclear equations printed in the original source.

### D. Summary flow

**Air enters the cow's lungs → oxygen diffuses into blood → blood carries oxygen to cells → cells release energy using oxygen → carbon dioxide returns in blood → carbon dioxide diffuses into alveoli → cow exhales.**

## 4. The neuron: structural and functional unit of nervous tissue

The nervous system receives information, processes it and coordinates responses. Nervous tissue contains two broad cell groups:

- **Neurons:** specialised cells that receive, process and transmit information using electrical signals and chemical communication at synapses.
- **Glial cells (neuroglia):** supporting cells that protect, nourish, insulate and help maintain the environment around neurons.

A **neuron** is the basic structural and functional unit of nervous tissue because it is the specialised cell that carries nerve impulses and communicates with other cells.

### Main parts of a typical neuron

| Part | Description and function |
|---|---|
| Cell body (soma) | Contains the nucleus and most of the cell's organelles; maintains the neuron and integrates incoming signals. |
| Dendrites | Usually branched extensions that receive signals from receptors or other neurons and carry them towards the cell body. |
| Axon | A usually single long extension that carries an electrical impulse away from the cell body towards target cells. |
| Myelin sheath | A fatty insulating covering formed by glial cells around many axons; it helps nerve impulses travel faster. |
| Nodes of Ranvier | Gaps between myelin segments that help rapid conduction along a myelinated axon. |
| Axon terminals | Branching ends of the axon that communicate with another neuron, muscle or gland at a synapse. |
| Synapse | The junction where a neuron communicates with another cell, usually using chemical messengers called neurotransmitters. |

### Direction of information flow

**Dendrites → cell body → axon → axon terminals → synapse → next cell**

This is the usual direction in a typical neuron. Not every neuron has exactly the same shape, but the diagram described here is a useful basic model.

### Three functional types of neuron

1. **Sensory (afferent) neuron:** carries information from a receptor towards the central nervous system.
2. **Interneuron (relay neuron):** connects neurons within the brain or spinal cord and helps process information.
3. **Motor (efferent) neuron:** carries commands from the central nervous system to an effector such as a muscle or gland.

## 5. Reflex action and the reflex arc

A **reflex action** is a rapid, automatic and involuntary response to a stimulus. It helps an animal respond to a change or possible danger without waiting for a deliberate decision.

A **reflex arc** is the pathway followed by nerve impulses during a reflex action.

### Five main parts of a reflex arc

1. **Receptor:** detects the stimulus, for example a sensory ending in the skin.
2. **Sensory neuron:** carries the impulse from the receptor towards the central nervous system.
3. **Integration centre:** the spinal cord or brainstem processes the information; one or more interneurons may connect sensory and motor pathways.
4. **Motor neuron:** carries an instruction away from the central nervous system.
5. **Effector:** a muscle or gland that produces the response.

### Example: withdrawal reflex

If a calf's foot receives a harmful stimulus, receptors detect it. A sensory neuron carries an impulse to the spinal cord. The spinal cord circuits activate motor neurons supplying flexor muscles. The muscles contract and the calf withdraws the limb.

The withdrawal response is protective. A spinal reflex does not mean that the animal has no conscious perception of pain; reflex movement and conscious pain behaviour are different observations.

### Four examples of reflex actions in animals

1. **Withdrawal reflex:** a calf withdraws a limb after a harmful stimulus to the hoof or foot.
2. **Suckling reflex:** a young calf responds to contact in the mouth by closing the mouth and moving the tongue to suckle.
3. **Blink or palpebral reflex:** an animal blinks when the eyelid region is lightly touched or the cornea is stimulated.
4. **Patellar (knee-jerk) reflex:** stimulation of the patellar tendon causes a brief extension movement at the stifle (knee) joint.

Other examples include the swallowing reflex, cough reflex, pupillary light reflex and anal/perineal reflex.

These are examples for learning, not instructions for testing animals. Do not pinch a calf, touch its eye or strike a tendon to demonstrate a reflex. Observe natural behaviour or use a teacher-approved video or veterinary demonstration.

## 6. Quick revision

- Inhalation: diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs move up and out; chest volume increases; lung pressure falls; air enters.
- Quiet exhalation: diaphragm relaxes; chest volume decreases; lung pressure rises; air leaves.
- In a cow, air passes through the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli.
- Oxygen diffuses from alveoli into blood; carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveoli.
- Blood carries oxygen to cells for aerobic cellular respiration.
- The neuron is the basic structural and functional unit of nervous tissue.
- Dendrites receive information; the cell body integrates it; the axon carries impulses away; axon terminals communicate at synapses.
- A reflex arc contains a receptor, sensory neuron, integration centre, motor neuron and effector.

## 7. Check your understanding

### Question 1 (8 marks)
Explain the mechanics of inhalation and quiet exhalation in a cow.

**Answer:** During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs up and out. The thoracic cavity increases in volume, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air enters. During quiet exhalation, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax. The chest and lungs recoil, thoracic volume decreases, lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Diaphragm action during inhalation and exhalation.
- 2 marks — External intercostal/rib movement during inhalation and exhalation.
- 2 marks — Correct volume and pressure changes.
- 2 marks — Correct direction of airflow in both phases.

### Question 2 (8 marks)
Trace the route of air in a cow from the nostrils to the gas-exchange surface. Explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

**Answer:** Air passes through the nostrils, nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air through the thin alveolar-capillary surface into blood and binds mainly to haemoglobin. Carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into the alveoli and is removed during exhalation.

**Marking:**
- 4 marks — Correctly traces the air route, with one mark for each group of structures in the correct sequence.
- 2 marks — Explains oxygen diffusion into blood and carriage by red blood cells.
- 2 marks — Explains carbon dioxide diffusion into alveoli and removal during exhalation.

### Question 3 (6 marks)
Describe how oxygen taken into a cow's lungs is used by its body cells.

**Answer:** Oxygen enters the alveoli and diffuses into the blood. Red blood cells carry it to tissues. Oxygen moves into cells, where it is used in aerobic cellular respiration to release energy from glucose. Carbon dioxide and water are produced; carbon dioxide enters the blood and is carried back to the lungs for exhalation.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Oxygen enters blood and is transported to tissues.
- 2 marks — Explains the use of oxygen in cellular respiration to release energy.
- 2 marks — Explains carbon dioxide production and transport back to the lungs.

### Question 4 (6 marks)
Define a neuron and describe the functions of the cell body, dendrites and axon.

**Answer:** A neuron is a specialised nerve cell and the basic structural and functional unit of nervous tissue. The cell body contains the nucleus and maintains the cell. Dendrites receive signals and carry them towards the cell body. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body towards other neurons, muscles or glands.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Defines a neuron and identifies its role as the basic unit.
- 1 mark — Cell body.
- 1 mark — Dendrites.
- 2 marks — Axon and direction of impulse transmission.

### Question 5 (5 marks)
List the five main parts of a reflex arc in the correct order.

**Answer:** Receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre (spinal cord or brainstem) → motor neuron → effector.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each correct part in the correct sequence.

### Question 6 (4 marks)
Give four examples of reflex actions in farm animals.

**Answer:** Any four accurate examples, such as withdrawal of a calf's limb, suckling reflex in a young calf, blink/palpebral reflex and patellar (knee-jerk) reflex. Swallowing, coughing, pupillary light and anal/perineal reflexes are also acceptable.

**Marking:** 1 mark for each correct example.

### Question 7 (3 marks)
Explain why a reflex action can occur before an animal makes a deliberate decision.

**Answer:** A receptor detects a stimulus and a nerve impulse travels along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord or brainstem. The central nervous system rapidly activates a motor neuron, which stimulates an effector. The response is automatic and does not require a deliberate decision first.

**Marking:**
- 1 mark — Receptor and sensory pathway.
- 1 mark — Integration in the spinal cord or brainstem.
- 1 mark — Motor pathway and automatic effector response.

**Total: 40 marks.** The marking criteria add up to the available marks for every question.

## References

1. Merck Veterinary Manual, The Respiratory System in Animals: https://www.merckvetmanual.com/respiratory-system/respiratory-system-introduction/the-respiratory-system-in-animals — mammalian airways, alveoli and gas exchange.
2. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, The Process of Breathing: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology/pages/22-3-the-process-of-breathing — pressure-volume changes, diaphragm and intercostal muscle actions during inhalation and exhalation.
3. OpenStax Anatomy and Physiology, Nervous Tissue: https://openstax.org/books/anatomy-and-physiology/pages/12-2-nervous-tissue — neuron structure, dendrites, cell body, axon, myelin and synapses.
4. NCBI Bookshelf, Physiology, Withdrawal Response: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544292/ — definition and protective role of the withdrawal reflex and reflex arc.
5. University of Wisconsin-Madison, Animal Science: Correction of Common Abnormal Presentations, Positions, and Postures: https://ansci.wisc.edu/jjp1/ansci_repro/lab/lab13_09/calving/abnormal_positions.html — calf withdrawal and suckle reflex examples.
6. Veterinary Practice News Canada, Making Sense of the Neuro Exam: https://www.veterinarypracticenews.ca/making-sense-of-the-neuro-exam/ — patellar, cranial tibial, withdrawal and perineal reflex examples.
7. Veterinary Practice News, Indicators used in livestock to assess unconsciousness after stunning: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4299535/ — blink, corneal, palpebral and pupillary reflexes in livestock.

Scientific facts are paraphrased. No source figure, textbook page or third-party diagram is reproduced. The original source's three displayed respiration equations and its respiratory/gill images are not modified or reused in this supplement.

practice.question: Explain the mechanics of inhalation and quiet exhalation in a cow.
practice.answer: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the external intercostal muscles contract and move the ribs up and out. Thoracic volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air enters. During quiet exhalation, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles relax. The chest and lungs recoil, thoracic volume decreases, lung pressure rises above atmospheric pressure and air flows out.

marking.criterion: Diaphragm action during inhalation and exhalation.
External intercostal/rib movement during inhalation and exhalation.
Correct volume and pressure changes.
Correct direction of airflow in both phases.

practice.question: Trace the route of air in a cow from the nostrils to the gas-exchange surface. Explain how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.
practice.answer: Air passes through the nostrils, nasal passages, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and bronchioles to the alveoli. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air through the thin alveolar-capillary surface into blood and binds mainly to haemoglobin. Carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into the alveoli and is removed during exhalation.

marking.criterion: Correctly traces the air route, with one mark for each group of structures in sequence.
Explains oxygen diffusion into blood and carriage by red blood cells.
Explains carbon dioxide diffusion into alveoli and removal during exhalation.

practice.question: Describe how oxygen taken into a cow's lungs is used by its body cells.
practice.answer: Oxygen enters the alveoli and diffuses into the blood. Red blood cells carry it to tissues. Oxygen moves into cells, where it is used in aerobic cellular respiration to release energy from glucose. Carbon dioxide and water are produced; carbon dioxide enters the blood and is carried back to the lungs for exhalation.

marking.criterion: Oxygen enters blood and is transported to tissues.
Explains the use of oxygen in cellular respiration to release energy.
Explains carbon dioxide production and transport back to the lungs.

practice.question: Define a neuron and describe the functions of the cell body, dendrites and axon.
practice.answer: A neuron is a specialised nerve cell and the basic structural and functional unit of nervous tissue. The cell body contains the nucleus and maintains the cell. Dendrites receive signals and carry them towards the cell body. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body towards other neurons, muscles or glands.

marking.criterion: Defines a neuron and identifies its role as the basic unit.
Explains the cell body.
Explains dendrites.
Explains axon and direction of impulse transmission.

practice.question: List the five main parts of a reflex arc in the correct order.
practice.answer: Receptor → sensory neuron → integration centre (spinal cord or brainstem) → motor neuron → effector.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct part in the correct sequence.

practice.question: Give four examples of reflex actions in farm animals.
practice.answer: Any four accurate examples, such as withdrawal of a calf's limb, suckling reflex in a young calf, blink/palpebral reflex and patellar (knee-jerk) reflex. Swallowing, coughing, pupillary light and anal/perineal reflexes are also acceptable.

marking.criterion: One mark for each correct example.

practice.question: Explain why a reflex action can occur before an animal makes a deliberate decision.
practice.answer: A receptor detects a stimulus and a nerve impulse travels along a sensory neuron to the spinal cord or brainstem. The central nervous system rapidly activates a motor neuron, which stimulates an effector. The response is automatic and does not require a deliberate decision first.

marking.criterion: Receptor and sensory pathway.
Integration in spinal cord or brainstem.
Motor pathway and automatic effector response.

lessons.title: Week Six supplement: sheep embryo development and normal lamb presentation
objectives: Describe the main stages of sheep embryo development from fertilisation through early implantation and foetal growth.
Explain the basic roles of foetal membranes and the placenta.
Distinguish fetal presentation, position and posture.
Describe the common normal presentation and posture of a lamb at birth.
Recognise that abnormal presentation or delayed progress requires a trained livestock professional or veterinarian.
lessons.body:
# Third Term, Week Six Supplement: Sheep Embryo Development and Normal Lamb Presentation

This supplement addresses the Week Six theory questions on embryo development and the normal position of a lamb before birth. It is for educational identification only. It is not a lambing procedure, veterinary diagnosis or guide to assisting delivery.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

1. Describe the main stages of sheep embryo development from fertilisation through early implantation and foetal growth.
2. Explain the basic roles of the foetal membranes and placenta.
3. Distinguish fetal presentation, position and posture.
4. Describe the common normal presentation and posture of a lamb at birth.
5. Recognise that abnormal presentation or delayed progress requires an experienced livestock professional or veterinarian.

## 1. From fertilisation to an embryo

**Fertilisation** occurs when a sperm cell joins with an ovum (egg cell) to form a single cell called a **zygote**. In sheep, fertilisation normally takes place in the oviduct (fallopian tube).

The zygote develops through a sequence of stages:

1. **Zygote:** the first cell formed after fertilisation. It contains genetic material from both parents.
2. **Cleavage:** the zygote divides repeatedly by mitosis to form smaller cells called blastomeres. The total conceptus does not initially grow much in size as these early divisions occur.
3. **Morula:** the developing embryo becomes a compact ball of cells. In sheep, it enters the uterus at approximately the morula stage.
4. **Blastocyst:** a fluid-filled cavity develops. Cells begin to organise into an inner cell mass, which forms the embryo proper, and an outer cell layer called the trophectoderm, which contributes to extra-embryonic tissues.
5. **Hatching and elongation:** the blastocyst sheds the protective zona pellucida. In sheep and other ruminants, the conceptus then elongates along the uterine surface.
6. **Attachment and implantation:** the trophoblast attaches to the uterine lining (endometrium). In sheep, implantation is a superficial attachment process; it is not the deep invasion seen in some other mammals.
7. **Embryonic development:** cells differentiate into the three primary germ layers—ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm. These layers give rise to the tissues and organs of the developing animal.
8. **Foetal growth:** after the main body plan and organ systems have begun to form, the developing young is described as a foetus. The foetus grows and its organs mature during the remainder of gestation.

### Simple development sequence

**Fertilisation → zygote → cleavage → morula → blastocyst → elongation and attachment to the uterus → embryo develops tissues and organs → foetus grows until birth.**

The sequence is more important for this lesson than memorising exact day numbers. Research reports approximate days for particular sheep breeds and study conditions; these timings should not be treated as identical for every ewe or pregnancy.

## 2. Foetal membranes and the placenta

The developing lamb is supported by extra-embryonic membranes and the placenta. These structures help protect the conceptus and support exchange between the ewe and the developing lamb.

| Structure | Main role |
|---|---|
| Amnion | Forms a membrane around the embryo/foetus and encloses amniotic fluid, which cushions and protects the developing young. |
| Chorion | The outer foetal membrane; contributes to the foetal part of the placenta and participates in exchange with maternal tissues. |
| Allantois | Helps form the chorioallantoic placenta and is involved in the handling of foetal waste during development. |
| Yolk sac | Supports very early development and contributes to early blood-cell and germ-cell development; it is not the main nutrient store for a sheep embryo as it is in a bird egg. |
| Placenta | Provides the interface for transfer of oxygen and nutrients from the ewe to the foetus and movement of carbon dioxide and waste products away from the foetus. |

In sheep, the placenta is **cotyledonary**. Specialised areas on the foetal membranes (cotyledons) connect with corresponding maternal structures in the uterus (caruncles). Together, these form placentomes, which are important sites of exchange.

The placenta is not simply a storage bag. It is an active exchange organ that supports the developing foetus while the foetus remains inside the uterus.

## 3. What happens during foetal development?

After the embryo has established contact with the uterus:

- cells continue to divide and specialise;
- the nervous system, skeleton, muscles and internal organs develop;
- the heart and blood vessels support circulation;
- the limbs, head and body become recognisable;
- the foetus grows as nutrients and oxygen are supplied through the placenta;
- organs continue to mature in preparation for life outside the uterus.

The developing lamb is enclosed by foetal membranes and surrounded by fluid. The uterus, placenta and membranes provide protection and support, but the foetus still depends on the ewe for oxygen and nutrients until birth.

## 4. Understanding lamb presentation, position and posture

These three words describe different aspects of how a foetus is arranged in the uterus and birth canal. They should not be used as if they mean the same thing.

### A. Presentation

**Presentation** describes how the long axis of the foetus lies in relation to the long axis of the ewe's birth canal.

- **Anterior (cranial) longitudinal presentation:** the lamb's head and forequarters are directed towards the birth canal. This is the common normal presentation in lambing.
- **Posterior (caudal) longitudinal presentation:** the lamb's hindquarters are directed towards the birth canal.
- **Transverse presentation:** the lamb lies across the uterus/birth canal rather than lengthwise.

### B. Position

**Position** describes how the lamb's back (dorsum) is oriented in relation to the ewe's pelvis.

- **Dorsosacral position:** the lamb's back is directed towards the ewe's sacrum (the upper, back part of the pelvic passage). This is the usual position in a normal anterior presentation.
- Other positions may be described by the direction of the lamb's back towards the ewe's side or pelvic bones. These require veterinary interpretation.

### C. Posture

**Posture** describes the arrangement of the lamb's head, neck and limbs in relation to its own body.

- **Normal anterior posture:** the head and neck are extended, and both forelimbs are extended forwards alongside the head.
- A flexed or retained limb, a head turned back, or limbs arranged abnormally is an abnormal posture, even if the lamb is still in anterior presentation.

## 5. Common normal presentation of a lamb

The most common normal presentation at lambing is:

- **Presentation:** anterior longitudinal — the head and forequarters are directed towards the birth canal.
- **Position:** dorsosacral — the lamb's back is oriented towards the ewe's sacrum.
- **Posture:** the head and neck are extended, with both forelimbs extended forwards and the nose positioned between or just ahead of the forelimbs.

This is often described as an **anterior dorsosacral presentation with normal posture**. Most lambs are delivered in this arrangement.

A posterior longitudinal presentation with the hindlimbs extended can also occur, but it is not the common normal presentation used for the basic classroom description. A transverse presentation, a head turned back or a retained limb is not the normal anterior posture.

### Remember the three terms

| Term | Question it answers | Normal lamb example |
|---|---|---|
| Presentation | Which end of the lamb is directed towards the birth canal? | Head/forequarters first (anterior) |
| Position | Which way is the lamb's back facing relative to the ewe's pelvis? | Back towards the ewe's sacrum (dorsosacral) |
| Posture | How are the head, neck and limbs arranged? | Head/neck and both forelimbs extended |

## 6. Recognising when professional help is needed

An abnormal presentation, position or posture can obstruct birth and endanger both ewe and lamb. Difficult birth is called **dystocia**.

Examples of abnormal findings include a head turned back, one or both forelimbs retained, hindquarters or tail appearing without the expected normal posture, or more than one lamb entering the birth canal together.

These are recognition terms only. Students must not attempt an internal examination, reposition a lamb, pull a lamb, use obstetrical instruments or administer medicines. If a real ewe appears to be having a difficult birth, the safe response is to alert the teacher, farm supervisor, experienced trained stockperson or veterinarian immediately. The professional decides whether and how assistance is required.

## 7. Quick revision

- Fertilisation forms a zygote.
- Cleavage produces blastomeres; a compact morula develops, followed by a blastocyst.
- The sheep blastocyst hatches and elongates before attaching to the uterine lining.
- Embryonic tissues differentiate; the embryo develops organs and becomes a growing foetus.
- Foetal membranes and placenta protect and support the developing lamb and enable exchange with the ewe.
- Presentation describes the long axis of the foetus relative to the birth canal.
- Position describes the orientation of the foetal back relative to the maternal pelvis.
- Posture describes the arrangement of the foetal head, neck and limbs.
- The common normal lamb presentation is anterior longitudinal, dorsosacral, with the head/neck and both forelimbs extended.
- Abnormal presentation or delayed progress is a veterinary/livestock-professional matter, not a student practical exercise.

## 8. Check your understanding

### Question 1 (8 marks)
Describe the main stages of sheep embryo development from fertilisation to the foetal stage.

**Answer:** Fertilisation joins the sperm and ovum to form a zygote. The zygote undergoes cleavage divisions to form blastomeres. The cells form a morula, which develops into a blastocyst. The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida, elongates and attaches to the uterine lining. Cells differentiate into germ layers and tissues/organs begin to form. The developing young is then described as a foetus, which grows and matures during gestation.

**Marking:**
- 1 mark — Fertilisation and zygote.
- 1 mark — Cleavage/blastomeres.
- 1 mark — Morula.
- 1 mark — Blastocyst.
- 1 mark — Hatching/elongation.
- 1 mark — Attachment/implantation.
- 1 mark — Differentiation and organ development.
- 1 mark — Foetal growth.

### Question 2 (6 marks)
State three functions of the foetal membranes or placenta in a pregnant ewe.

**Answer:** The amnion encloses protective amniotic fluid that cushions the foetus. The chorion and allantois contribute to the foetal part of the placenta. The placenta enables oxygen and nutrients to pass from the ewe to the foetus and allows carbon dioxide and wastes to move away from the foetus.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Protection/cushioning by amnion and amniotic fluid.
- 2 marks — Contribution of chorion/allantois to the placenta.
- 2 marks — Exchange of oxygen/nutrients and removal of carbon dioxide/waste.

### Question 3 (6 marks)
Distinguish between presentation, position and posture in a lamb.

**Answer:** Presentation describes which end of the lamb is directed towards the birth canal. Position describes the direction of the lamb's back relative to the ewe's pelvis. Posture describes how the lamb's head, neck and limbs are arranged relative to its own body.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Correct meaning of presentation.
- 2 marks — Correct meaning of position.
- 2 marks — Correct meaning of posture.

### Question 4 (6 marks)
Describe the common normal presentation, position and posture of a lamb at birth.

**Answer:** The common normal arrangement is anterior longitudinal presentation, dorsosacral position and normal posture. The lamb's head and forequarters are directed towards the birth canal; its back faces the ewe's sacrum; and its head, neck and both forelimbs are extended forwards.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Anterior longitudinal presentation.
- 2 marks — Dorsosacral position.
- 2 marks — Head/neck and both forelimbs extended.

### Question 5 (6 marks)
Explain why the placenta is important to a developing lamb.

**Answer:** The placenta connects the foetal membranes with the ewe's uterine tissues. It provides a surface for oxygen and nutrients to pass to the foetus and for carbon dioxide and metabolic wastes to move away. It supports foetal growth while the lamb is inside the uterus.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Explains connection/interface between foetal and maternal tissues.
- 2 marks — Explains supply of oxygen and nutrients.
- 2 marks — Explains removal of carbon dioxide/wastes and support of growth.

### Question 6 (4 marks)
Give two examples of abnormal fetal posture or presentation that may cause difficulty at lambing.

**Answer:** Examples include a head turned back, one or both forelimbs retained/flexed, breech presentation, transverse presentation or two lambs entering the birth canal together.

**Marking:** 2 marks for each correct example.

### Question 7 (4 marks)
A student observes that a ewe is straining but the lamb is not progressing and an abnormal presentation may be present. State the appropriate safe response for a student.

**Answer:** The student should alert the teacher, farm supervisor, trained experienced stockperson or veterinarian immediately. The student must not carry out an internal examination, reposition the lamb, pull it, use obstetrical instruments or administer medicines.

**Marking:**
- 2 marks — Promptly alerts an appropriate trained professional.
- 2 marks — States that the student must not attempt internal examination, repositioning, extraction or treatment.

**Total: 40 marks.** Each marking guide adds up to the marks available for the question.

## References

1. University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine, Drost Project: The Visual Guide to Ovine Reproduction — Presentation: https://visgar.vetmed.ufl.edu/en_ovirep/presentation/presentation.html — identifies the common normal lamb arrangement as anterior presentation, dorsosacral position and normal posture. The lesson uses the textual veterinary description only; no site image is reproduced.
2. University of Florida College of Veterinary Medicine, Drost Project: The Visual Guide to Ovine Reproduction — Normal Lambing: https://visgar.vetmed.ufl.edu/en_ovirep/normal-lambing/normal-lambing.html — veterinary visual guide to normal lambing and foetal membranes. No site images are reproduced.
3. Early Embryonic Development in Agriculturally Important Species (peer-reviewed review, 2024), section 3.1 Pregnancy in Sheep: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11240814/ — describes cleavage, morula, blastocyst, hatching and elongation in sheep.
4. Spencer et al., Implantation mechanisms: insights from the sheep (Reproduction, 2004): https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15579583/ — describes blastocyst development and superficial attachment to the uterine lining in domestic ruminants.
5. Lambing Management and Neonatal Care (peer-reviewed veterinary review): https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7149567/ — describes normal anterior dorsosacral lamb presentation with the forelimbs extended and neonatal considerations.
6. Merck Veterinary Manual, Parturition in Goats: https://www.merckvetmanual.com/management-and-nutrition/management-of-reproduction-goats/parturition-in-goats — veterinary context for common cranial/dorsosacral presentation in small ruminants; the lesson's primary sheep description is based on ovine-specific sources.

This supplement is educational and non-procedural. It does not provide lamb repositioning, extraction, assisted-delivery, treatment or medication instructions. No source images or diagrams are copied. An independent named veterinary reviewer has not signed off this repository lesson; veterinary review remains a required approval gate before learner release.
